children.title: Concave Quadratic Minimization
children.top_down_role: The all-nonpositive-curvature regime over bounded convex or polyhedral domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave Quadratic Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional concave quadratic minimization over compact convex sets, with the polyhedral extreme-point property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\), where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\preceq0\). Then \(q\) is concave on \(C\), and \(\min_{x\in C}q(x)\) is attained. If \(C=P\) is a polytope, at least one global minimizer is an extreme point of \(P\); equivalently, \[\min_{x\in P}q(x)=\min_{v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)}q(v).\] The assertion does not imply that every minimizer is extreme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave quadratic attains its minimum on a compact convex set; over a polytope, some global minimizer is a vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(C=P\) is polyhedral and bounded, then \(\min_{x\in P}q(x)=\min_{v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)}q(v)\).

notation.meaning: Set of extreme points of the polytope.

source_refs.locator: 4. Basic Properties of Concave Minimization Problems p. 58
1.1.2 Concave Minimization p. 6

source_witnesses.locator: 4. Basic Properties of Concave Minimization Problems p. 58
1.1.2 Concave Minimization p. 6

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite method for a polytope supplied by a finite generating list.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v^1,\ldots,v^N\}\) and \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\), where \(Q\preceq0\). Evaluating every \(q(v^i)\) and returning a least-valued generator produces a global minimizer over \(P\). With dense quadratic data, the evaluations require \(O(Nn^2)\) arithmetic operations. A polytope given by inequalities can have exponentially many vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave quadratic over a finitely generated polytope is solved by testing all generators, but an inequality description may have exponentially many vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i^*\in\arg\min_i q(v^i)\Longrightarrow v^{i^*}\in\arg\min_{x\in P}q(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Vertex Enumeration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict concavity supplies neither local-to-global sufficiency nor uniqueness for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=-x^2\) on \([-1,2]\), the endpoint \(-1\) is a strict relative local minimizer but \(q(-1)=-1>q(2)=-4\). On \([-1,1]\), the same strictly concave quadratic has the two global minimizers \(-1\) and \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly concave quadratic can have a nonglobal local minimum and multiple global minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Strict concavity implies neither local-to-global minimality nor uniqueness of a minimum.}
knowledge_statements.title: Local and Unique-Minimum Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why the seed's attainment conclusion cannot be extended to arbitrary convex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=-x^2\) on the bounded convex but nonclosed set \((-1,1)\), \(\inf q=-1\) is not attained. On the closed unbounded convex set \(\mathbb R\), the same concave quadratic is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without compactness, a concave quadratic minimum may be unattained or unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in(-1,1)}q(x)=-1\text{ is unattained},\qquad \inf_{x\in\mathbb R}q(x)=-\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compact-convex extension of the polytope vertex result in the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(q\) be concave and continuous on \(C\). Then some global minimizer of \(q\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ext}(C)\), so \[\min_{x\in C}q(x)=\min_{v\in\operatorname{ext}(C)}q(v).\] This asserts existence of an extreme minimizer, not that every minimizer is extreme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous concave function on a finite-dimensional compact convex set has an extreme-point global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}q(x)\cap\operatorname{ext}(C)\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: Extreme points of the compact convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Minimum Principle

children.title: Fully Indefinite Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Objectives containing both positive- and negative-curvature subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Indefinite Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by the simultaneous presence of positive and negative objective curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\) over a feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\). The program is fully indefinite when \(Q\) has at least one strictly positive and at least one strictly negative eigenvalue, equivalently when there exist nonzero directions \(d_+\) and \(d_-\) satisfying \(d_+^{\mathsf T}Qd_+>0\) and \(d_-^{\mathsf T}Qd_-<0\). Thus the objective is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully indefinite QP has both positive- and negative-curvature directions, so its objective is neither globally convex nor globally concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The program is fully indefinite exactly when \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)<0<\lambda_{\max}(Q)\).

source_refs.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38

source_witnesses.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38

children.title: Restricted-Negative-Inertia Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Models parameterized by a fixed or small number of negative-curvature directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Negative-Inertia Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indefinite quadratic programs parameterized by a positive, bounded number of negative Hessian eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\) with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), define the negative inertia \(\nu_-(Q)\) as the number of strictly negative eigenvalues of \(Q\), counted with multiplicity. For a prescribed parameter \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a restricted-negative-inertia quadratic program satisfies \(1\leq\nu_-(Q)\leq k\). Equivalently, the maximal dimension of a subspace \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0\) for every nonzero \(d\in S\) lies between \(1\) and \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These QPs have at least one and at most a prescribed number of independent negative-curvature directions, measured by the Hessian's negative inertia.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restricted negative inertia means \(1\leq\nu_-(Q)\leq k\).

notation.meaning: Number of strictly negative eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix, counted with multiplicity.
Upper bound on the positive number of negative-curvature directions.
Subspace on which the quadratic form is strictly negative away from the origin.

children.top_down_role: Continuous domains whose boundedness, faces, or quadratic boundaries alter the global structure.

children.title: Affine-Geometry Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Quadratic optimization governed by projected spectral curvature and recession behavior.

children.title: Unconstrained Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Spectral curvature, finite optima, unboundedness, plus stationary behavior without explicit constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct decision and solution procedure for an unconstrained quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute \(Q=U\Lambda U^{\mathsf T}\) and \(g=U^{\mathsf T}c\). If some \(\lambda_i<0\), \(u_i\) is a negative-curvature unboundedness witness. If all \(\lambda_i\ge0\) but \(g_i\ne0\) for some \(\lambda_i=0\), a signed \(u_i\) gives linear escape to \(-\infty\). Otherwise choose \(z_i=-g_i/\lambda_i\) for \(\lambda_i>0\), arbitrary \(z_i\) for \(\lambda_i=0\), and return \(x=Uz\). Standard dense arithmetic costs \(O(n^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An eigendecomposition returns either a minimizer or an explicit negative-curvature or null-slope witness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure exactly decides boundedness and constructs a minimizer or unboundedness witness.

notation.meaning: Linear coefficient in the Hessian eigenbasis.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Boundedness and Solution Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete classification by Hessian inertia.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Qx_*+c=0\). Then \(x_*\) is a local minimum if and only if \(Q\succeq0\), in which case it is global, and it is strict if and only if \(Q\succ0\). Analogously it is a local maximum if and only if \(Q\preceq0\), strict if and only if \(Q\prec0\). If \(Q\) has positive and negative eigenvalues, every stationary point is a saddle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hessian inertia completely classifies stationary points of an unconstrained quadratic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The definiteness class of \(Q\) determines whether \(x_*\) is a minimum, maximum, or saddle.
knowledge_statements.title: Classification of Unconstrained Stationary Points
Unconstrained Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundedness and solution characterization for a symmetric unconstrained quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\). The infimum of \(q\) is finite if and only if \(Q\succeq0\) and \(c\in\operatorname{Range}(Q)\). Under these conditions the minimizers are exactly the solutions of \(Qx=-c\), and \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}q(x)=\alpha-\tfrac12c^{\mathsf T}Q^{\dagger}c.\] Otherwise \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}q(x)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained quadratic is bounded below exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite and its linear coefficient lies in the Hessian range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite attainment holds exactly when \(Q\succeq0\) and \(c\in\operatorname{Range}(Q)\), with minimizers satisfying \(Qx=-c\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundedness, minimizer, and pseudoinverse-value theorem is mathematically standard and precisely stated, but no inspectable source is supplied for this nontrivial exact characterization.

children.title: Affine-Subspace Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Quadratic optimization restricted to translated linear subspaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct solution after null-space reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose feasible \(x_0\) and a null-space basis \(N\), and form \(H=N^{\mathsf T}QN\), \(h=N^{\mathsf T}(Qx_0+c)\). If \(H\succeq0\) and \(h\in\operatorname{Range}(H)\), solve \(Hz=-h\) and return \(x_*=x_0+Nz\). A negative eigenvalue of \(H\), or a vector \(d\in\ker H\) with \(h^{\mathsf T}d\ne0\), certifies unboundedness below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected linear system solves the finite case, while projected negative curvature or a null slope certifies unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: A feasible point and a basis of \(\ker A\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced solve returns a global minimizer exactly in the finite regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Linear-System Solution

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global-optimality certificate on an affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha:Ax=b\}\), suppose \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd\ge0\) for every \(d\in\ker A\). A feasible \(x_*\) is globally optimal if and only if there exists \(y\) such that \[Qx_*+c+A^{\mathsf T}y=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected positive semidefiniteness makes the equality-constrained KKT equations necessary and sufficient for global optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible \(x_*\) is optimal exactly when \(Qx_*+c\in\operatorname{Range}(A^{\mathsf T})\).
knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Curvature KKT Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact uniqueness criterion in the finite regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume a minimizer exists. It is unique if and only if \[d^{\mathsf T}Qd>0\quad\text{for every }0\ne d\in\ker A.\] Equivalently, \(N^{\mathsf T}QN\succ0\). If the reduced Hessian is singular and the problem is bounded below, minimizers form an affine family along its null directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimizer is unique exactly when curvature is positive on every nonzero feasible direction.
assumptions_latex: The affine feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniqueness is equivalent to positive definiteness of \(Q\) on \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness from Positive Feasible-Direction Curvature
Affine-Subspace Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Null-space reduction and boundedness characterization for equality-constrained quadratic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\), choose \(x_0\in F\), and let the columns of \(N\) form a basis of \(\ker A\). Every feasible point is \(x=x_0+Nz\), and \[q(x_0+Nz)=q(x_0)+h^{\mathsf T}z+\tfrac12z^{\mathsf T}Hz,\qquad H=N^{\mathsf T}QN,\quad h=N^{\mathsf T}(Qx_0+c).\] Consequently, the affine-subspace problem is bounded below exactly when \(H\succeq0\) and \(h\in\operatorname{Range}(H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameterizing an affine feasible set by a null-space basis reduces the problem to an unconstrained quadratic with a projected Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced problem has Hessian \(H=N^{\mathsf T}QN\) and is bounded below exactly when \(H\succeq0\) and \(h\in\operatorname{Range}(H)\).

notation.meaning: Matrix whose columns form a basis for the feasible-direction subspace.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The null-space representation and projected boundedness characterization are correct, but the record supplies no source for the exact representation and if-and-only-if claim.

children.title: Projected-Recession Boundary
children.top_down_role: Projected curvature plus feasible recession structures controlling boundedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Recession Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular projected curvature separates coercive affine restriction from flat or linearly unbounded recession behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the affine reduction \(x=x_0+Nz\), let \(H=N^{\mathsf T}QN\) and \(h=N^{\mathsf T}(Qx_0+c)\). The projected-recession boundary is the case \(H\succeq0\) with \(\ker H\neq\{0\}\). For any \(d\in\ker H\), the reduced objective along \(z+td\) changes by \(t h^{\mathsf T}d\). Hence, if some such \(d\) satisfies \(h^{\mathsf T}d\neq0\), the infimum is \(-\infty\); if \(h\perp\ker H\), the objective is flat along null directions and has finite minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At singular projected curvature, a nonzero linear slope along a null direction causes unboundedness; orthogonality instead produces flat minimizer directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite boundedness on the boundary holds exactly when \(h\perp\ker H\), equivalently \(h\in\operatorname{Range}(H)\).

notation.meaning: Hessian restricted to affine feasible directions.
Linear coefficient of the reduced quadratic.
Projected recession direction in the null space of the reduced Hessian.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular projected-Hessian boundary statement is mathematically consistent, but neither the exact characterization nor the local term “projected-recession boundary” has an inspectable source.

children.title: Box-Constrained Indefinite Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Coordinate-bounded models supporting separable envelopes and spatial subdivision.

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained Indefinite Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indefinite quadratic minimization over a finite coordinate box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A box-constrained indefinite quadratic program has the form \[\min\left\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha:\ell_i\leq x_i\leq u_i,\ i=1,\ldots,n\right\},\] where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) has at least one negative eigenvalue and every bound is finite with \(\ell_i<u_i\). The feasible box is compact, so the continuous objective attains a global minimum despite its nonconvexity. Coordinate bounds also provide finite intervals for constructing convex envelopes and spatial subdivisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This model minimizes a nonconvex quadratic over finite coordinate intervals; compactness guarantees existence of a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is compact and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{\ell\leq x\leq u}q(x)\neq\varnothing\).

source_refs.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38
Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

source_witnesses.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38
Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary first-order conditions on a finite box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=Qx_*+c\). At every local minimizer, \[g_i=0\ \text{if }\ell_i<x_{*i}<u_i,\qquad g_i\ge0\ \text{if }x_{*i}=\ell_i,\qquad g_i\le0\ \text{if }x_{*i}=u_i.\] Equivalently, \(0\in Qx_*+c+N_{[\ell,u]}(x_*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient components vanish in the interior and have the appropriate sign at active bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinatewise bound-stationarity conditions hold.

notation.meaning: Normal cone of the box at \(x_*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise First-Order Conditions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of first-order stationarity in the nonconvex regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{-x^2:-1\le x\le1\}\), the interior point \(x=0\) satisfies first-order box stationarity but is a strict local maximum; the global minima are \(x=\pm1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box-stationary point of a nonconvex quadratic can be a strict maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: First-order box stationarity is not sufficient for local or global optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Box Stationarity Is Not Sufficient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Attainment for Multi-Affine Box Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-rounding property for zero diagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q_{ii}=0\) for every \(i\), the objective is affine in each coordinate separately. Successively choosing a nonincreasing endpoint for each coordinate yields a vertex \(v\) with \(q(v)\le q(x)\). Hence \[\min_{x\in[\ell,u]}q(x)=\min_{v_i\in\{\ell_i,u_i\}}q(v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-affine quadratic over a box always has a vertex minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous and vertex-restricted minimum values coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Attainment for Multi-Affine Box Quadratics

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Attainment for Concave Box Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point reduction for the concave subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q\preceq0\), then on a finite box \([\ell,u]\), \[\min_{x\in[\ell,u]}q(x)=\min_{v_i\in\{\ell_i,u_i\}}q(v).\] Thus at least one global minimizer is a box vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave quadratic attains its box minimum at a vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A global minimizer exists among the box vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Attainment for Concave Box Quadratics

children.title: Polyhedrally Constrained Indefinite Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Linear-constraint models shaped by active faces, vertices, and recession directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedrally Constrained Indefinite Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indefinite quadratic minimization over a polyhedron described by finitely many affine inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedrally constrained indefinite quadratic program is \[\min\left\{q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha:Ax\leq b\right\},\] where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) has a negative eigenvalue and the polyhedron \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\) is nonempty. If \(P\) is bounded, continuity ensures global attainment. If \(P\) is unbounded, boundedness of the objective must additionally be checked along feasible recession directions in \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad\leq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family minimizes an indefinite quadratic over linear inequalities; unbounded polyhedra require analysis of feasible recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(P\) is bounded, a global minimizer exists; otherwise recession behavior can determine whether the infimum is finite.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the feasible polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38

source_witnesses.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local curvature restriction at a polyhedral local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=Qx_*+c\) and \[C(x_*)=\{d\in T_P(x_*):g^{\mathsf T}d=0\}.\] At every local minimizer, \[g^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\quad(d\in T_P(x_*)),\qquad d^{\mathsf T}Qd\ge0\quad(d\in C(x_*)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible tangent directions cannot descend, and zero-slope feasible directions cannot have negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: First-order tangent-cone and second-order critical-cone necessary conditions hold.

notation.meaning: Critical cone of zero first-order feasible directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Cone Second-Order Necessity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Frank–Wolfe Attainment Theorem for Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment of a finite quadratic infimum on a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron, \(q\) is quadratic, and \(\inf_{x\in P}q(x)>-\infty\), then there exists \(x_*\in P\) satisfying \[q(x_*)=\inf_{x\in P}q(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every quadratic bounded below on a nonempty polyhedron attains its minimum there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}q(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Frank–Wolfe Attainment Theorem for Quadratic Programs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex Attainment for Concave Quadratic Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point property on a compact polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope and \(Q\preceq0\), then \[\min_{x\in P}q(x)=\min_{v\in\operatorname{ext}(P)}q(v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave quadratic minimized over a compact polytope has an optimal vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some extreme point of \(P\) globally minimizes \(q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Attainment for Concave Quadratic Minimization

children.title: Quadratically Constrained QP Interface
children.top_down_role: The boundary between objective-only nonconvex QP and general nonconvex QCQP.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constraint Curvature Alone Does Not Classify a Particular Sublevel Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of curvature-only inference at the QP-to-QCQP boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In one dimension, \(-x^2\le0\) has feasible set \(\mathbb R\), whereas \(1-x^2\le0\) has feasible set \(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\). Both Hessians are negative. Thus non-PSD curvature removes the general convexity guarantee but does not alone determine whether a particular quadratic sublevel set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-PSD constraint curvature can produce either a convex or nonconvex sublevel set.
assumptions_latex: Constraints are interpreted as sublevel inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Non-PSD curvature alone neither proves nor disproves convexity of a particular quadratic sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Curvature Alone Does Not Classify a Particular Sublevel Set
Quadratically Constrained QP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal boundary between quadratic objectives with affine constraints and quadratically constrained quadratic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A quadratic program with objective \(q_0(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x+c_0^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_0\) remains an objective-only nonconvex QP when every constraint is affine. It crosses into QCQP when at least one constraint has the form \[q_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+c_i^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha_i\leq0\] with \(Q_i\neq0\). Such a constraint defines a convex sublevel set when \(Q_i\succeq0\); without this condition, the feasible-set geometry may itself be nonconvex, independently of \(Q_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QP becomes a QCQP once a genuine quadratic constraint is introduced; indefinite constraint curvature may add feasible-set nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface is crossed exactly when some constraint has \(Q_i\neq0\); its sublevel set is guaranteed convex when \(Q_i\succeq0\).

source_refs.locator: 2.6.4 Nonlinearly Constrained Convex Sets p. 127

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6.4 Nonlinearly Constrained Convex Sets p. 127

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical distinction and convex-sublevel claim are standard, but the cited locator concerns nonlinearly constrained convex sets and does not directly establish the asserted QP-to-QCQP classification boundary.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex-QCQP theorem, whose canonical home is the QCQP definition topic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimizing \(q_0(x)\) subject to \(q_i(x)\le0\) and affine equalities, positive-semidefinite objective and inequality Hessians give a convex optimization problem. Nonaffine quadratic equalities are excluded from the standard convex-QCQP form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PSD objective and inequality Hessians with affine equalities define a convex QCQP.
assumptions_latex: Quadratic inequalities use the sublevel convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated curvature and equality conditions are sufficient for convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex QCQP Boundary

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is the QP-to-QCQP classification boundary and the warning that non-PSD constraint curvature removes a guarantee rather than exactly classifying each sublevel set. The proposed general convex-QCQP condition was deferred as duplication of the general QCQP definition node. Box, polyhedral, and affine QPs remain sibling scopes; QCQP algorithms, duality, and exactness theorems remain downstream.

children.title: Structured Indefinite-QP Families
children.top_down_role: Problem families whose product pattern, separability, or sparsity supports specialized analysis.

children.title: Bilinear Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Quadratic models whose nonconvexity lies in products between variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-variable quadratic models whose coupling is a bilinear product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilinear quadratic objective over \(X\times Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q\) has the form \(f(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}My+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+\alpha\). With \(z=(x,y)\), it admits the quadratic representation \[f(x,y)=\tfrac12z^{\mathsf T}\begin{pmatrix}0&M\\M^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}z+\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf T}z+\alpha.\] If \(M\neq0\), the block Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues; nevertheless, \(f\) is affine in either block when the other is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear program couples two variable blocks through products; its joint Hessian is indefinite although each one-block restriction is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(M\neq0\), the joint Hessian is indefinite while each fixed-block restriction is affine.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Bilinear Programming Problems p. 69

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Bilinear Programming Problems p. 69

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point principle for separately affine objectives on compact convex product domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) be nonempty compact convex sets and let \(f(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}My+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+\alpha\). Both a global minimum and a global maximum are attained at some pair in \(\operatorname{ext}(X)\times\operatorname{ext}(Y)\). Hence \[\min_{X\times Y}f=\min_{\operatorname{ext}(X)\times\operatorname{ext}(Y)}f,\qquad \max_{X\times Y}f=\max_{\operatorname{ext}(X)\times\operatorname{ext}(Y)}f.\] For polytopes these reduce to finite vertex-pair searches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear-affine objective over compact convex product domains has minimum and maximum solutions at pairs of extreme points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact convex sets.
\(f\) is affine in each block separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{X\times Y}f\cap(\operatorname{ext}(X)\times\operatorname{ext}(Y))\ne\varnothing,\quad \operatorname*{argmax}_{X\times Y}f\cap(\operatorname{ext}(X)\times\operatorname{ext}(Y))\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: Extreme points of the two block domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Pair Attainment

children.title: Biconvex Quadratic Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic families exhibiting convexity within individual variable blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Biconvex Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-Hessian criterion for separate convexity of a quadratic objective on a product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be convex, and consider \[f(x,y)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_xx+x^{\mathsf T}My+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}Q_yy+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+\alpha,\] with symmetric \(Q_x\) and \(Q_y\). The function is biconvex on \(X\times Y\) when \(f(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\) and \(f(x,\cdot)\) is convex on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). On full-dimensional domains, this holds exactly when \(Q_x\succeq0\) and \(Q_y\succeq0\); no definiteness condition on \(M\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block quadratic is biconvex exactly when both diagonal Hessian blocks are positive semidefinite; the cross-block coupling is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Biconvexity is equivalent to \(Q_x\succeq0\) and \(Q_y\succeq0\).

source_refs.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

source_witnesses.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical descent property and limited convergence guarantee for compact-domain biconvex quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be nonempty compact sets and let \(f\) be continuous and convex in each block separately. Starting from \((x^0,y^0)\), choose \[x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in X}f(x,y^k),\qquad y^{k+1}\in\arg\min_{y\in Y}f(x^{k+1},y).\] Then \[f(x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\le f(x^{k+1},y^k)\le f(x^k,y^k).\] Consequently the objective values converge because they are nonincreasing and bounded below. Biconvexity alone does not imply convergence of the iterates or global optimality of their limit points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact alternating minimization decreases the objective and has convergent values on compact domains, but biconvexity alone gives no global or iterate-convergence guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Each block subproblem is solved globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\le f(x^k,y^k)\quad\text{and}\quad \{f(x^k,y^k)\}\text{ converges}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Alternating Block Minimization

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise Optimality Is Not Global Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure boundary for alternating reasoning in biconvex quadratic models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x,y)=xy\) on \([-1,1]^2\). The function is affine, hence convex, in either block with the other fixed. At \((0,0)\), every \(x\) minimizes \(f(x,0)\) and every \(y\) minimizes \(f(0,y)\), so \((0,0)\) is coordinatewise minimizing. Nevertheless, \(f(0,0)=0\), while the global minimum is \(-1\), attained at \((-1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\). An exact alternating method may therefore remain at a suboptimal tied block solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear biconvex model can have a coordinatewise minimum that is not globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (0,0)\text{ is coordinatewise minimizing but }f(0,0)>\min_{[-1,1]^2}f.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Optimality Is Not Global Optimality

children.title: Convex-Concave Quadratic Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic families organized by opposing curvature components.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Concave Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-Hessian criterion for quadratic functions convex in one block and concave in another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be convex, and define \[f(x,y)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_xx+x^{\mathsf T}My+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}Q_yy+a^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+\alpha,\] where \(Q_x\) and \(Q_y\) are symmetric. The function is convex-concave when \(f(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), while \(f(x,\cdot)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). On full-dimensional domains, this is equivalent to \(Q_x\succeq0\) and \(Q_y\preceq0\), independently of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block quadratic is convex-concave when its first diagonal Hessian block is positive semidefinite and its second is negative semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convex-concavity is equivalent to \(Q_x\succeq0\) and \(Q_y\preceq0\).

notation.meaning: Hessian with respect to the convex block.
Hessian with respect to the concave block.

source_refs.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

source_witnesses.locator: 9.3.1 Biconvex and Convex-Concave Programming p. 190

children.title: Blockwise-to-Saddle Interface
children.top_down_role: Regimes where blockwise convex structure induces or fails to induce saddle structure.

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(R\in\mathbb S_+^m\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y)=L(x^*,y^*)\) for a saddle point \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connects a convex-concave quadratic block model to its saddle-point and minimax formulation.

source_refs.locator: 2.12.2 Saddle Point of a Function p. 75

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty compact convex sets. Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(R\in\mathbb S_+^m\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d\in\mathbb R^m\), and define \[L(x,y)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+x^{\mathsf T}Ay-\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}Ry+c^{\mathsf T}x+d^{\mathsf T}y.\] Then \(L\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\). A pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point exactly when \[L(x^*,y)\le L(x^*,y^*)\le L(x,y^*)\quad\text{for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y.\] Under these hypotheses, at least one saddle point exists and \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y)=L(x^*,y^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous convex-concave quadratic payoff on nonempty compact convex block domains, a saddle point exists and its value equals both orders of min-max optimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise-to-Saddle Interface

source_witnesses.locator: 2.12.2 Saddle Point of a Function p. 75

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variational-inequality certificate for differentiable convex-concave payoffs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be nonempty convex sets and let \(L\) be differentiable, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). A feasible pair \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point if and only if \[\langle\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*),x-x^*\rangle\ge0\quad(\forall x\in X),\qquad \langle\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*),y-y^*\rangle\le0\quad(\forall y\in Y).\] For the seed's quadratic payoff, the gradients are \(Qx^*+Ay^*+c\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}x^*-Ry^*+d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible pair is a saddle point exactly when its block gradients satisfy the minimization and maximization variational inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is differentiable, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^*,y^*)\text{ is a saddle point}\iff\begin{cases}\langle\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*),x-x^*\rangle\ge0&\forall x\in X,\\\langle\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*),y-y^*\rangle\le0&\forall y\in Y.\end{cases}
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Saddle Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness or an appropriate coercive substitute is needed for the seed's unconditional existence conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(0,1)\), \(Y=\{0\}\), and \(L(x,0)=x\). The payoff is affine and therefore convex-concave, but its infimum over \(X\times Y\) is \(0\) and is not attained. Hence no saddle point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex-concave curvature alone does not ensure saddle attainment on a noncompact domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in X}L(x,0)=0\text{ is unattained, so no saddle point exists}.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Existence Boundary Without Compactness

children.title: Decomposable Block-Structured Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Models admitting componentwise envelopes or block decomposition.

children.title: Separable Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Models whose nonconvex quadratic structure decomposes by individual components.

assumptions_latex: \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\) is a fixed block partition with \(x_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The program is separable precisely when \(X=\prod_{i=1}^pX_i\) and \(q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^pq_i(x_i)\); for a quadratic objective, the latter condition is equivalent to block-diagonality of its Hessian in the fixed partition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines full objective-and-feasible-set separability across coordinate blocks.

source_refs.locator: 4.4 DC Representation of Separable Functions p. 110

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the variables be partitioned as \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\), with \(x_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}\). A quadratic program is separable across this partition if its feasible set is a Cartesian product \(X=\prod_{i=1}^pX_i\) and its objective can be written as \[q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p q_i(x_i),\qquad q_i(x_i)=\tfrac12x_i^{\mathsf T}Q_ix_i+c_i^{\mathsf T}x_i+\alpha_i.\] For a quadratic objective, objective separability is equivalent to block-diagonality of the Hessian after the simultaneous row and column permutation induced by the partition. Block-diagonality alone does not imply separability of the whole program unless the feasible set also has the stated product form. The matrices \(Q_i\) may be indefinite; separability concerns coupling, not convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic program is separable when both its objective and feasible set split across blocks. Block-diagonality characterizes objective separability, while full program separability additionally requires product feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Quadratic Programs

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4 DC Representation of Separable Functions p. 110

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact serial or parallel solution procedure induced by full separability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Independently solve \(v_i=\inf_{x_i\in X_i}q_i(x_i)\) for every block. If a block certifies \(v_i=-\infty\), report the full problem unbounded below. If every block returns a global minimizer \(x_i^*\), return \(x^*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_p^*)\) with value \(\sum_iq_i(x_i^*)\). If block \(i\) requires work \(T_i\), total block-solution work is \(\sum_iT_i\) serially; in an ideal independent-task parallel model with one processor per block, its depth is \(\max_iT_i\), apart from aggregation overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the blocks independently and combine their optimizers and values; the independent solves may run in parallel.
assumptions_latex: The objective and feasible set are fully separable in the stated partition.
Each block solver is globally valid for its block problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assembled point is globally optimal, or a block unboundedness certificate proves the full problem unbounded below.

notation.meaning: Work required by the solver for block i

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Block Solution Algorithm

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Product Decomposition of the Global Optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global value, solution-set, attainment, and unboundedness decomposition for a fully separable quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{i=1}^pX_i\), where every \(X_i\neq\varnothing\), and let \(q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p q_i(x_i)\), with every \(q_i\) real-valued on \(X_i\). Then \[\inf_{x\in X}q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p\inf_{x_i\in X_i}q_i(x_i)\] in the extended reals. If the common value is finite, \(x^*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_p^*)\) is a global minimizer if and only if \(x_i^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x_i\in X_i}q_i(x_i)\) for every \(i\). Thus the finite infimum is attained exactly when every block infimum is attained, and the full problem is unbounded below exactly when at least one block is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global value is the sum of the block values, and finite global minimizers are exactly the Cartesian products of block minimizers. One unbounded block makes the full problem unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_Xq=\sum_i\inf_{X_i}q_i\), with componentwise characterizations of finite attainment and unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Product Decomposition of the Global Optimum

children.title: Block-Structured Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Models organized by interacting variable blocks or blockwise curvature.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dualization of additive linking constraints exposes independent block quadratic subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^p q_i(x_i):x_i\in X_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^p A_i x_i=b,\ \sum_{i=1}^p g_i(x_i)\le0\right\}.
\]
For an equality multiplier \(y\) and an inequality multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\), the Lagrangian dual function separates as
\[
\theta(y,\lambda)=-b^{\mathsf T}y+
\sum_{i=1}^p\inf_{x_i\in X_i}
\bigl(q_i(x_i)+y^{\mathsf T}A_i x_i+\lambda^{\mathsf T}g_i(x_i)\bigr).
\]
Thus \(\theta(y,\lambda)\) is a valid lower bound computed from independent block subproblems. Equality with the primal optimum requires an applicable strong-duality condition and is not guaranteed for a nonconvex block QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing additive linking constraints separates a block QP into independent Lagrangian subproblems and gives a global lower bound, although nonconvexity may leave a duality gap.
assumptions_latex: The objective and nonlinking terms are block additive.
\(\lambda\ge0\) corresponds to componentwise inequality linking constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta(y,\lambda)\le v_\star\), and \(\theta\) equals a constant plus a sum of independent block infima.
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Recovery of Block Separability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition induced by connected components of the complete objective-and-constraint incidence structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Partition \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\). Form a hypergraph on \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\) containing an edge \(\{i,j\}\) whenever the objective has a nonzero cross block \(Q_{ij}\), and the block scope \(S_a\) of every constraint. If its connected components are \(C_1,\ldots,C_t\), then
\[
F=\prod_{r=1}^tF_r,\qquad q(x)=\alpha+\sum_{r=1}^tq_r(x_{C_r}).
\]
In extended-real form,
\[
\inf_{x\in F}q(x)=\alpha+
\sum_{r=1}^t\inf_{z_r\in F_r}q_r(z_r).
\]
When all component minima are attained, concatenating component minimizers gives a global minimizer; infeasibility of any component makes the whole program infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connected components of the combined Hessian and constraint-scope hypergraph yield independent optimization components whose values add and whose attained minimizers concatenate.
assumptions_latex: Every constraint has an explicitly specified block scope \(S_a\).
No objective or constraint term spans distinct connected components.
Component infima are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_Fq=\alpha+\sum_r\inf_{F_r}q_r\), with componentwise feasibility and optimizer assembly when minima are attained.

notation.meaning: Set of variable blocks occurring in constraint a
Connected component of the combined interaction hypergraph

knowledge_statements.title: Connected-Component Decomposition Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational decomposition from explicitly supplied objective and constraint block incidences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form a hypergraph on blocks \(1,\ldots,p\), adding \(\{i,j\}\) for every nonzero off-diagonal Hessian block \(Q_{ij}\) and a hyperedge \(S_a\) for each constraint scope. Compute its connected components \(C_1,\ldots,C_t\), assign each objective term and constraint to its component, and solve the resulting component programs independently. If \(M\) is the total listed incidence size, hypergraph construction and component detection take \(O(p+M)\) time. Sequential solution takes \(O(p+M)+\sum_rT_r\); independent components may instead be solved in parallel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The combined interaction hypergraph can be decomposed in linear incidence time, after which its independent component programs can be solved separately.
assumptions_latex: Every cross-block objective interaction and constraint scope is explicitly enumerated.
No term or constraint spans distinct computed components.
Each component is solved to the accuracy required for the original program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{detect}}=O(p+M),\qquad T_{\mathrm{sequential}}=O(p+M)+\sum_{r=1}^tT_r.

notation.meaning: Cost of solving component subproblem r

review_flags: The summed solver cost is a sequential bound; parallel wall-clock cost depends on scheduling and resources.
knowledge_statements.title: Interaction-Component Decomposition Procedure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregation of Componentwise Global Bounds and Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global certificates obtained after exact interaction-component decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F=\prod_{r=1}^tF_r\) and \(q(x)=\alpha+\sum_{r=1}^tq_r(x_{C_r})\). If \(L_r\le\inf_{F_r}q_r\) and \(\hat x_r\in F_r\), then \[L:=\alpha+\sum_{r=1}^tL_r\le\inf_Fq,\qquad U:=\alpha+\sum_{r=1}^tq_r(\hat x_r)=q(\hat x),\] where \(\hat x=(\hat x_1,\ldots,\hat x_t)\in F\), and \[U-L=\sum_{r=1}^t\bigl(q_r(\hat x_r)-L_r\bigr).\] Hence zero component gaps certify global optimality of the assembled point, while nonzero component gaps give an additive absolute-error certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent components, valid lower bounds, feasible objective values, and absolute gaps add; zero component gaps certify global optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(L_r\) is a valid global lower bound for component \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\le v_\star\le U,\qquad U-L=\sum_{r=1}^t\bigl(q_r(\hat x_r)-L_r\bigr).

notation.meaning: Valid global lower bound for component r

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation of Componentwise Global Bounds and Gaps
Block-Structured Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines quadratic programs whose data respect a prescribed variable-block interaction pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\), write a quadratic objective as \[q(x)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p x_i^{\mathsf T}Q_{ij}x_j+\sum_{i=1}^pc_i^{\mathsf T}x_i+\alpha,\qquad Q_{ji}=Q_{ij}^{\mathsf T}.\] The program is block structured when a prescribed graph \(G=(\{1,\ldots,p\},E)\) satisfies \(Q_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i\ne j\) and \(\{i,j\}\notin E\), and each constraint involves variables from a specified small collection of blocks. It is block separable precisely when \(E=\varnothing\) and the feasible set is a Cartesian product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-structured quadratic program restricts quadratic and constraint coupling to specified block interactions; complete block separation is the zero-coupling special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Off-pattern blocks satisfy \(Q_{ij}=0\), and constraint scopes respect the prescribed block pattern.

notation.meaning: Hessian block coupling variable blocks i and j

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

children.title: Componentwise Envelope Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structures supporting localized envelopes across components.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible-Set Coupling Invalidates Componentwise Envelope Assembly
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact nonproduct-domain witness showing that independently computed component envelopes need not form the exact envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{(0,0),(1,1),(2,0)\}\), let \(f(x_1,x_2)=f_1(x_1)+f_2(x_2)\), and prescribe \(f_1(0)=f_1(2)=0\), \(f_1(1)=-1\), and \(f_2(0)=f_2(1)=0\). At \(z=(1,0)\in\operatorname{conv}(X)\), every convex representation of \(z\) by points of \(X\) uses only \((0,0)\) and \((2,0)\), so \(\operatorname{clconv}_X f(z)=0\). In contrast, the independently computed component envelopes on the coordinate projections give \(\operatorname{clconv}_{\{0,1,2\}}f_1(1)+\operatorname{clconv}_{\{0,1\}}f_2(0)=-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a coupled compact domain, independently convexifying additive coordinate functions can give a strict underestimate of the true envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{clconv}_X f(1,0)=0>-1=\operatorname{clconv}_{\operatorname{proj}_1X}f_1(1)+\operatorname{clconv}_{\operatorname{proj}_2X}f_2(0)\).

notation.meaning: Projection of X onto coordinate i

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Coupling Invalidates Componentwise Envelope Assembly

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional formulation procedure once exact component envelopes are available on a product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{i=1}^pX_i\) and \(f(x)=\sum_i f_i(x_i)\). Suppose an exact closed convex-envelope epigraph formulation \(E_i=\{(x_i,t_i):x_i\in\operatorname{conv}(X_i),\ t_i\ge e_i(x_i)\}\) is available for every component. Under the product-envelope identity \(\operatorname{clconv}_Xf(x)=\sum_i e_i(x_i)\), an exact epigraph formulation is obtained by taking all component formulations independently and imposing \(t\ge\sum_it_i\). If formulation \(E_i\) has size \(s_i\), the uncoupled assembled formulation has size \(O(\sum_i s_i+p)\), before optional shared-variable elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact component-envelope epigraphs assemble by juxtaposition plus one summation inequality, with additive formulation size, provided the product-envelope identity holds.
assumptions_latex: Each \(E_i\) exactly represents the epigraph of the corresponding component closed convex envelope.
The product-envelope identity holds for the stated domains and functions.
All formulation sizes use a common additive encoding convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{clconv}_Xf)=\{(x,t):\exists t_i,\ (x_i,t_i)\in E_i,\ t\ge\sum_it_i\}\).

notation.meaning: Exact epigraph formulation of component envelope i
Encoding size of component formulation i

review_flags: Conditional on the product-envelope identity, which remains an immutable deferred seed.
knowledge_statements.title: Assembly of Exact Component-Envelope Formulations
Componentwise Envelope Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when convexification of a separable objective reduces exactly to componentwise envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{i=1}^pX_i\), where every \(X_i\) is nonempty and compact, and let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^pf_i(x_i)\), with each \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\) lower semicontinuous. On \(\operatorname{conv}(X)=\prod_i\operatorname{conv}(X_i)\), the closed convex envelope separates as \[\operatorname{clconv}_{X}f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p\operatorname{clconv}_{X_i}f_i(x_i).\] Consequently, a separable indefinite quadratic over a box or product domain can be convexified block by block. Objective or feasible-set coupling generally invalidates this identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an additive objective on a product domain, the closed convex envelope equals the sum of the component envelopes; coupling can destroy this decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{clconv}_{X}f=\sum_i\operatorname{clconv}_{X_i}f_i\).

notation.meaning: Closed convex envelope of f relative to X

children.title: Block-Decomposition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interaction patterns determining whether block decomposition remains useful.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Decomposition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies cross-block constraints as a sharp obstruction to independent block minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Additivity of the objective alone does not justify independent block optimization. Let \(X_1=X_2=[0,1]\), \(f_i(x_i)=x_i^2\), and impose the coupling constraint \(x_1+x_2=1\). Each isolated block problem has the unique minimizer \(x_i=0\), so the concatenated blockwise solution \((0,0)\) is infeasible. The coupled problem instead has the unique minimizer \((1/2,1/2)\). Thus the identity \[\min_{x\in\prod_iX_i}\sum_i f_i(x_i)=\sum_i\min_{x_i\in X_i}f_i(x_i)\] applies to product feasibility, but need not survive even one linear cross-block constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent block minimization fails under cross-block constraints: a two-variable separable quadratic with one coupling equality already has incompatible blockwise minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The blockwise point \((0,0)\) is infeasible, while the coupled minimizer is \((1/2,1/2)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit elementary counterexample verifies the stated decomposition failure

children.title: Sparse Indefinite Quadratic Programs
children.top_down_role: Models with limited quadratic interaction graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Indefinite Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines indefinite quadratic programs whose objective and constraint data have sparse incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sparse indefinite quadratic program has the form \[\min_{x\in X}\ q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha,\] where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) has at least one negative eigenvalue and the numbers of nonzero entries in \(Q\) and in the matrices defining \(X\) are small relative to their ambient dimensions. The sparsity graph of the objective has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and edge \(\{i,j\}\) whenever \(i\ne j\) and \(Q_{ij}\ne0\). Sparsity restricts variable interactions but does not imply convexity or a small number of negative eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse indefinite quadratic program combines negative curvature with few nonzero objective and constraint coefficients; sparsity alone does not limit nonconvexity.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is specified by sparse data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is sparse in data incidence but remains nonconvex because \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)<0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Large-Scale Indefinite Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the operator-data sense of large scale, avoiding an arbitrary dimension threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A large-scale indefinite quadratic program is a problem \[\min_{x\in X}\ \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\] with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)<0\), for which dense storage or factorization of the full problem data is outside the intended computational model. Accordingly, \(Q\), constraint Jacobians, and relaxations are accessed through sparse representations, decompositions, or matrix-vector oracles. The designation is computational rather than dimension-invariant: it depends on available memory, data structure, and the permitted linear-algebra operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large-scale indefinite QP is too large for dense treatment in its computational setting and therefore uses sparse, decomposed, or matrix-free data access.
assumptions_latex: Dense storage or factorization is excluded by the computational setting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Problem data must be accessed through structured, sparse, decomposed, or matrix-free operations.

notation.meaning: Indefinite objective Hessian or its operator representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal operator interface for evaluating a large-scale quadratic objective and its derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\) with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), an operator product \(y=Qx\) gives \[q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}y+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha,\qquad \nabla q(x)=y+c,\] while \(\nabla^2q(x)v=Qv\). Thus objective, gradient, and Hessian-vector evaluations need only applications of the \(Q\)-operator and vector operations, not explicit dense storage or factorization. This interface alone supplies neither a global lower bound nor a global-optimality certificate for an indefinite QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hessian operator suffices for quadratic and derivative evaluations, but operator access alone does not solve or certify the global nonconvex problem.
assumptions_latex: An oracle or structured routine computes \(Qv\) for requested vectors \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective and derivative evaluation can be matrix-free, while global certification requires additional structure or relaxation machinery.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Quadratic Evaluation Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns recognition of optimality for a supplied point, rather than merely computing a stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonconvex quadratic program and a specified feasible point $\bar x$, deciding whether $\bar x$ is a global minimizer is NP-hard. Deciding whether a specified point is a local minimizer of a nonconvex QP is also NP-hard. In contrast, convex quadratic programming admits algorithms with polynomial complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonconvex quadratic programming, it is NP-hard to decide whether a given feasible point is a global minimizer, and it is also NP-hard to decide whether a given point is a local minimizer. Convex QP, by contrast, has polynomial-complexity algorithms.

\bar x\text{ is a specified feasible point for the global-minimum recognition problem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Decide}(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}q)\text{ is NP-hard},\qquad \operatorname{Decide}(\bar x\text{ is a local minimizer})\text{ is NP-hard}.

children.title: Small Nonconvex-Core Regimes
children.top_down_role: Large models whose indefinite curvature is concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Small Nonconvex-Core Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents negative curvature through a low-dimensional factor while retaining a convex quadratic remainder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) admit a decomposition \[Q=P-UU^{\mathsf T},\qquad P\succeq0,
\quad U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r},\quad r\ll n.\] Then the quadratic objective satisfies \[\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Px+c^{\mathsf T}x-\tfrac12\lVert U^{\mathsf T}x\rVert_2^2.\] Hence all explicitly concave dependence is mediated by the \(r\)-dimensional image \(z=U^{\mathsf T}x\); on every affine fiber with fixed \(z\), the displayed objective is convex in \(x\). When \(r\) equals the negative inertia of \(Q\), this gives a minimal-dimensional negative-curvature core.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the Hessian is a positive-semidefinite matrix minus a low-rank Gram matrix, nonconvexity is confined to a low-dimensional projected variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonconvex dependence is confined to \(z=U^{\mathsf T}x\in\mathbb R^r\), and fixed-\(z\) fibers have convex quadratic objectives.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Low-Dimensional Curvature Is Not Alone an Algorithmic Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the exact structural reduction from a tractability conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(Q=P-UU^{\mathsf T}\) with small \(r=\operatorname{rank}(U)\) confines explicitly concave dependence to \(z\in\mathbb R^r\), but alone gives no polynomial-time global-solution bound. An algorithmic conclusion additionally requires effective solution of the fiber problems defining \(\phi(z)\), a usable representation or oracle for \(Z=U^{\mathsf T}X\), and a global method for minimizing \(\phi(z)-\tfrac12\|z\|^2\) over \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small negative-curvature core is a structural parameter, not an automatic tractability theorem; the fibers and projected domain must also be manageable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Small core dimension alone does not imply a polynomial-time global algorithm.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the represented nonconvex core

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Dimensional Curvature Is Not Alone an Algorithmic Guarantee

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Reduction to the Nonconvex-Core Image
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-function reduction from ambient variables to the low-dimensional negative-curvature image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Q=P-UU^{\mathsf T}\) with \(P\succeq0\). Define \(h(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Px+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\), \(Z=U^{\mathsf T}X\), and \[\phi(z)=\inf\{h(x):x\in X,\ U^{\mathsf T}x=z\}.\] Then \[\inf_{x\in X}\left(h(x)-\tfrac12\|U^{\mathsf T}x\|_2^2\right)=\inf_{z\in Z}\left(\phi(z)-\tfrac12\|z\|_2^2\right).\] If \(X\) is convex, \(\phi\) is an extended-real convex function. When the relevant outer and fiber infima are attained, an outer minimizer and an optimal corresponding fiber point recover a global minimizer of the original QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization over fibers gives an exact problem in the low-dimensional core variable; a convex feasible set gives a convex fiber-value function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original infimum equals \(\inf_{z\in Z}(\phi(z)-\tfrac12\|z\|^2)\), with optimizer recovery through an attained optimal fiber.

notation.meaning: Image of the feasible set under the core projection
Optimal value of the positive-semidefinite-curvature fiber problem

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Reduction to the Nonconvex-Core Image

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-curvature working-set step for an indefinite quadratic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded indefinite-QP specialization of a feasible active-set method; the precise constraint orientation is inherited from referenced problem (9.1.1)–(9.1.3).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $
abla Q(x_k)=g+Gx_k$. Choose $d_k$ such that $a_i^Td_k=0$ for all $i\in S_k$ and either $d_k^TGd_k<0$, or $d_k^TGd_k=0$ and $
abla Q(x_k)^Td_k<0$. If $a_i^Td_k\geq0$ for every $i
otin S_k$, then problem (9.1.1)--(9.1.3) is unbounded below. Otherwise, choose $\alpha_k$ as large as possible while keeping $x_k+\alpha_kd_k$ feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a direction tangent to the working-set constraints that has negative curvature, or zero curvature and a negative directional derivative. If the direction remains feasible for every inactive constraint, the original problem is unbounded below. Otherwise, take the largest step that preserves feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall i\notin S_k,\ a_i^Td_k\geq0\right]\Rightarrow\text{the original problem is unbounded below};\quad\left[\exists i\notin S_k,\ a_i^Td_k<0\right]\Rightarrow\alpha_k=\max\{\alpha\geq0:x_k+\alpha d_k\text{ is feasible}\}

children.title: Sparsity-Scale Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: The effect of sparse interaction structure on large-instance global difficulty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Arrowhead Condensation Can Create Dense Fill
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates sparse input storage from elimination and Schur-complement fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[Q=\begin{pmatrix}a&b^{\mathsf T}\\b&D\end{pmatrix},\] where \(a\ne0\), \(D\) is diagonal, and every entry of \(b\in\mathbb R^{n-1}\) is nonzero. Then \(Q\) has \(O(n)\) structural nonzeros. Eliminating the first variable produces \[S=D-a^{-1}bb^{\mathsf T},\] whose every off-diagonal entry is nonzero. Thus this ordering creates \(\Theta(n^2)\) structural nonzeros. Sparse input size alone therefore does not guarantee sparse factorization or inexpensive condensation; ordering and elimination-graph structure also matter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arrowhead Hessian has linear input sparsity, but eliminating its hub creates a dense Schur complement.
assumptions_latex: Structural fill is counted without numerical cancellation.
The first variable is eliminated first.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{nnz}(Q)=O(n)\) while \(\operatorname{nnz}(S)=\Theta(n^2)\) for the specified ordering.

notation.meaning: Schur complement after eliminating the first variable

review_flags: The separation concerns the specified ordering; alternative orderings may produce less fill.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Arrowhead Condensation Can Create Dense Fill

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition under which sparsity remains compatible with controlled direct-elimination cost as dimension grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix have a fixed elimination ordering whose filled graph has at most \(w\) later neighbors at every vertex. If elimination proceeds with that symbolic pattern and all required pivots exist, the factor has \(O(nw)\) stored entries and elimination uses \(O(nw^2)\) arithmetic operations. Uniformly bounded filled width therefore gives linear storage and work in \(n\); a small input nonzero count alone does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded filled elimination width, not input sparsity alone, controls sparse-factorization storage and work.
assumptions_latex: A fixed symmetric elimination ordering has filled width at most \(w\).
All required pivots exist for elimination with the stated pattern.
Additional fill or delayed pivots introduced for numerical stability is excluded from the count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{storage}=O(nw),\qquad \operatorname{work}=O(nw^2).

notation.meaning: Maximum later-neighbor count in the filled elimination graph

review_flags: Stability-driven pivoting can change the symbolic pattern and bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Width Sparse Elimination Bound

assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is stored in a standard sparse format.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication costs \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(Q))\), but sparsity does not force \(n_-(Q)\) to be small, and small \(n_-(Q)\) does not force \(Q\) to be sparse.

notation.meaning: Number of stored nonzero entries of Q
Number of negative eigenvalues counted with multiplicity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates sparse linear-algebra cost from the dimension of negative curvature without denying elementary dimension-dependent bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric matrix \(Q\) stored in a standard sparse format, computing \(Qx\) from its stored nonzeros costs \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(Q))\) arithmetic operations and uses \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(Q))\) matrix storage. Sparsity does not force the negative-inertia count \(n_-(Q)\) to be small relative to the dimension: \(Q=-I_n\) has \(n\) nonzeros and \(n_-(Q)=n\). Conversely, small negative inertia does not imply sparsity: for any vector \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) with all entries nonzero, \(Q=I_n-2uu^{\mathsf T}/(u^{\mathsf T}u)\) is dense and has \(n_-(Q)=1\). Thus sparse linear-algebra cost is governed by \(\operatorname{nnz}(Q)\), whereas negative-curvature decompositions are governed by \(n_-(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse matrix operations scale with the number of stored nonzeros, but a sparse matrix can have negative curvature in every dimension, while a dense matrix can have only one negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity-Scale Tradeoff
