children.title: Feasible-Descent Directions
children.top_down_role: Locally feasible directions that expose improvement from a candidate point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Quadratic Descent Test Along a Feasible Ray
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient local descent classification for a fixed straight-line feasible direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\), let \(x\in F\), and suppose a nonzero \(d\) satisfies \(x+td\in F\) for every \(t\in[0,\varepsilon]\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\). Set \(a=\nabla q(x)^{\mathsf T}d\) and \(b=d^{\mathsf T}Qd\). Then \(q(x+td)<q(x)\) for all sufficiently small \(t>0\) if and only if \[a<0\quad\text{or}\quad(a=0\ \text{and}\ b<0).\] If \(a>0\), or if \(a=0\) and \(b\ge0\), the fixed ray does not strictly decrease the objective for every sufficiently small positive step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a locally feasible ray, a quadratic decreases exactly when its first-order slope is negative, or its slope is zero and its curvature is negative.
assumptions_latex: The segment \(x+td\) is feasible for every sufficiently small \(t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed ray is locally descending iff \(\nabla q(x)^{\mathsf T}d<0\), or \(\nabla q(x)^{\mathsf T}d=0\) and \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Quadratic Descent Test Along a Feasible Ray
Feasible-Descent Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines straight-line feasible directions that strictly decrease a quadratic objective locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(x\in F\), and let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha\) with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\). A nonzero vector \(d\) is a feasible-descent direction at \(x\) if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(x+td\in F\) and \(q(x+td)<q(x)\) for every \(t\in(0,\varepsilon]\). Since \[q(x+td)-q(x)=t\nabla q(x)^{\mathsf T}d+\tfrac12t^2d^{\mathsf T}Qd,\] every feasible direction satisfying \(\nabla q(x)^{\mathsf T}d<0\) is a feasible-descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible-descent direction stays feasible along a short ray and strictly lowers the quadratic objective; a negative directional derivative guarantees descent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility of the short ray and \(\nabla q(x)^{\mathsf T}d<0\) imply strict local descent along \(d\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: follows from the exact quadratic expansion

children.title: Tangent Geometry
children.top_down_role: First-order feasible-set geometry near quadratic-program candidates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linearized-Cone Outer Approximation and Abadie Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint representation of tangent geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x:g_i(x)\le0,\ h_j(x)=0\}\), where the constraints are differentiable at \(\bar x\in F\), and let \(I(\bar x)=\{i:g_i(\bar x)=0\}\). Define \[L_F(\bar x)=\{d:\nabla g_i(\bar x)^\top d\le0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),\ \nabla h_j(\bar x)^\top d=0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}.\] Then \(T_F(\bar x)\subseteq L_F(\bar x)\). Abadie's constraint qualification at \(\bar x\) is the equality \(T_F(\bar x)=L_F(\bar x)\); without it the inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearized cone outer-approximates the tangent cone, and Abadie's qualification is equality of these cones.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is represented by finitely many constraints differentiable at \(\bar x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_F(\bar x)\subseteq L_F(\bar x)\), with equality exactly under ACQ.
knowledge_statements.title: Linearized-Cone Outer Approximation and Abadie Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Tangent and Regular Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polarity relation intrinsic to first-order feasible geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C^\circ=\{v:v^\top d\le0\ \forall d\in C\}\), the regular normal cone satisfies \[\widehat N_F(x)=T_F(x)^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular normal cone is the negative polar of the Bouligand tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_F(x)=T_F(x)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Tangent and Regular Normal Cones

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Cone Structure of the Bouligand Tangent Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic structure; convexity is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in F\), \(T_F(x)\) is closed, contains \(0\), and satisfies \(d\in T_F(x),\ \alpha\ge0\Rightarrow\alpha d\in T_F(x)\). It need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand tangent cone is a closed cone containing zero, but can be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_F(x)\) is a closed, not necessarily convex, cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Cone Structure of the Bouligand Tangent Cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential-free equivalent formulation of the contingent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in F\), \[d\in T_F(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x+td,F)}{t}=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is tangent exactly when its infinitesimal ray approaches the feasible set with sublinear error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_F(x)=\{d:\liminf_{t\downarrow0}t^{-1}\operatorname{dist}(x+td,F)=0\}.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from y to F

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Characterization of Tangency
Tangent Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the Bouligand contingent cone for possibly nonconvex feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in F\). The Bouligand tangent cone to \(F\) at \(x\) is \[T_F(x)=\left\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\ \exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ \exists\,x_k\in F\text{ with }x_k\to x\text{ and }\frac{x_k-x}{t_k}\to d\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(d\in T_F(x)\) when there are perturbations \(d_k\to d\) and positive steps \(t_k\downarrow0\) such that \(x+t_kd_k\in F\). The cone records first-order feasible velocities and need not be convex when \(F\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand tangent cone consists of limits of scaled feasible displacements and captures all first-order feasible velocities, including for nonconvex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_F(x)\) is the cone of limits of scaled feasible displacements from \(x\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to F at x
Positive step sequence converging to zero

children.title: Descent-Tangent Compatibility
children.top_down_role: The relation between improving directions plus tangent approximations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Tangent Derivative Is Inconclusive for Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary showing that neutral tangent directions need not generate strict descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=x^2\), and \(\bar x=0\). Then \(T_F(0)=\mathbb R\) and \(\nabla f(0)d=0\) for every \(d\in T_F(0)\), yet \(f(t)=t^2\ge f(0)\) for every \(t\). Thus tangent membership together with zero first-order derivative does not imply the existence of nearby strict descent points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the minimum of x squared every tangent direction has zero first-order derivative, but none produces strict descent; neutrality alone is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\in T_F(0)\) and \(\nabla f(0)d=0\) do not imply nearby feasible strict descent.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Tangent Derivative Is Inconclusive for Descent

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative Tangent Slope Is Sufficient but Not Necessary for Nearby Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp converse boundary for the tangent-slope descent implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=-x^2\), and \(\bar x=0\). For \(d=1\in T_F(0)\), \(\nabla f(0)^{\mathsf T}d=0\), but for every \(t>0\), \(\bar x+td=t\in F\) and \(f(t)=-t^2<f(0)\). Thus nearby feasible strict descent can exist even though the corresponding first-order tangent slope is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative tangent slope guarantees descent, but negative second-order curvature can produce descent when the first-order slope is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(0)^{\mathsf T}d=0\) while \(f(td)<f(0)\) for every \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Negative Tangent Slope Is Sufficient but Not Necessary for Nearby Descent
Descent-Tangent Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates negative tangent directional derivatives to feasible descent sequences and first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(x\in F\), and let \(f\) be differentiable at \(x\). If \(d\in T_F(x)\) and \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then there exist \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(d_k\to d\) such that \(x+t_kd_k\in F\) and \(f(x+t_kd_k)<f(x)\) for all sufficiently large \(k\). Consequently, every local minimizer satisfies \[\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\qquad\text{for every }d\in T_F(x).\] When the directional derivative is zero, tangent membership alone gives no strict-descent conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangent direction with negative directional derivative yields nearby feasible descent; therefore every local minimizer has nonnegative derivative on its tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local minimality implies \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\) for all \(d\in T_F(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard first-order consequence of differentiability and contingent tangency

children.title: Directional Stationarity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Geometric separation between directionally stationary candidates plus improvable points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Stationarity Is Not Sufficient for Local Minimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp nonconvex boundary of the first-order tangent-cone condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(q(x)=-x^2\) on \(F=\mathbb R\) at \( ar x=0\). Since \(T_F(0)=\mathbb R\) and \(
abla q(0)=0\), \[
abla q(0)d=0\ge0\qquad	ext{for every }d\in T_F(0),\] so \(0\) is directionally stationary and every tangent direction is neutral. Nevertheless, \(q(t)=-t^2<q(0)\) for every \(t
eq0\), so \(0\) is a strict local maximizer and not a local minimizer.

Directional Stationarity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order boundary between feasible descent and neutral tangent directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed, let \(f\) be differentiable at \( ar x\in F\), and let \(T_F( ar x)\) be the Bouligand tangent cone. Directional stationarity is the condition \[
abla f( ar x)^	op d\ge 0\quad	ext{for every }d\in T_F( ar x).\] Its boundary consists of the neutral feasible directions \[\mathcal B( ar x)=\{d\in T_F( ar x):
abla f( ar x)^	op d=0\}.\] If some \(d\in T_F( ar x)\) satisfies \(
abla f( ar x)^	op d<0\), then \( ar x\) is not a local minimizer.

KKT Points of Indefinite Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT system for a quadratically constrained indefinite quadratic objective.

Consider \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(h_j(x)=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\), where all functions are quadratic and the Hessian of \(f\) need not be positive semidefinite. abla g_i( ar x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x)=0,\qquad \lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive Lagrangian curvature in every nonzero critical direction yields a uniform curvature bound, quadratic growth, and strict local minimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-Hessian sufficiency and the indefinite-QP multiplicity boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict local optimality for linearly constrained QPs and the loss of global landscape simplicity outside the positive-definite regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) be a feasible KKT point of a linearly constrained QP, let \(\mathcal A(x^*)\) be its active set, and let the columns of \(Z\) form a basis for \(\{d:a_i^Td=0\ \forall i\in\mathcal A(x^*)\}\). If \(Z^TGZ\succ0\), then \(x^*\) is a strict local minimizer. Outside the positive-definite curvature regime, in particular when \(G\) is indefinite, the class of linearly constrained QPs can have more than one strict local minimizer and can also contain local maximizers and other stationary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible KKT point, positive definiteness of the Hessian reduced to the null space of the active-constraint Jacobian guarantees a strict local minimum. Indefinite quadratic programs need not have a unique local minimum and may exhibit several strict local minima together with local maxima or other stationary points.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is a feasible KKT point}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is a strict local minimizer};\qquad G\text{ indefinite }\Longrightarrow\text{ multiple strict local minimizers may occur in the problem class}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Critical-Cone Curvature Implies a Strict Local Minimum for an Indefinite QP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indefinite-QP specialization of the source's second-order sufficient condition for linearly constrained quadratic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x \tfrac12x^TGx+g^Tx\) subject to \(a_i^Tx=b_i\) for \(i\in E\) and \(a_i^Tx\ge b_i\) for \(i\in I\), where \(G=G^T\) is indefinite. Let \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) be a KKT pair, let \(I(x^*)=\{i\in I:a_i^Tx^*=b_i\}\), and define \[\mathcal G(x^*,\lambda^*)=\{d\ne0:a_i^Td=0\ (i\in E),\ a_i^Td\ge0\ (i\in I(x^*)),\ a_i^Td=0\ (i\in I(x^*),\lambda_i^*>0)\}.\] If \(d^TGd>0\) for every \(d\in\mathcal G(x^*,\lambda^*)\), then \(x^*\) is a strict local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an indefinite linearly constrained QP, a KKT point is a strict local minimizer if the Hessian has strictly positive curvature along every nonzero direction in the associated critical cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is a strict local minimizer.}

children.title: Quadratic-Growth Isolation Principle
children.top_down_role: Growth, isolation, and stability consequences associated with strict curvature.

children.title: Quadratic Growth
children.top_down_role: Local objective separation associated with strict feasible curvature.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality defines quadratic growth and implies that \(\bar x\) is a strict local minimizer over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local objective growth of second order relative to distance from a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\bar x\in F\), and let \(f:F\to\mathbb R\). The objective \(f\) has quadratic growth at \(\bar x\) over \(F\) if there exist constants \(c>0\) and \(r>0\) such that \[f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+c\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in F\text{ with }\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\le r.\] The constants are local and need not provide a bound outside the ball of radius \(r\). Quadratic growth implies that \(\bar x\) is a strict local minimizer over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth means every nearby feasible point has objective value at least a positive quadratic distance above the candidate value.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth

children.title: Isolated Local Minima
children.top_down_role: Local minimizers separated from neighboring minimizing candidates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is an isolated strict local minimizer exactly when it uniquely minimizes \(f\) on some feasible closed ball centered at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: closed Euclidean ball of radius r centered at the candidate point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of an isolated strict local minimizer
terminology_note: some sources distinguish isolated local minimizer from isolated strict local minimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict local minimizer separated from all other feasible points with equal or lower objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and let \(f:F\to\mathbb R\). A point \(\bar x\in F\) is an isolated strict local minimizer if there exists \(r>0\) such that \[f(x)>f(\bar x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in F\text{ satisfying }0<\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\le r.\] Equivalently, \(\bar x\) is the unique minimizer of \(f\) over \(F\cap\overline B_r(\bar x)\). Quadratic growth at \(\bar x\) implies this isolation property, although isolation alone does not specify a quadratic growth rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isolated strict local minimizer is the unique minimizer within some feasible neighborhood; quadratic growth guarantees this property.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolated Local Minima

children.title: Growth-to-Isolation Implications
children.top_down_role: Conditions linking local growth behavior to minimizer isolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth-to-Isolation Implications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic growth makes the reference point the unique minimizer in a neighborhood, isolating it within that neighborhood's minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\bar x\in X\). If there exist \(\alpha>0\) and \(r>0\) such that
\[
f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\alpha\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^2
\quad\text{for every }x\in X\cap B_r(\bar x),
\]
then every distinct \(x\in X\cap B_r(\bar x)\) satisfies \(f(x)>f(\bar x)\). Hence \(\bar x\) is a strict local minimizer and the unique minimizer of \(f\) over \(X\cap B_r(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive quadratic-growth bound makes the reference point a strict local minimizer and the unique minimizer in the specified neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The displayed quadratic-growth inequality holds for some \(\alpha,r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is the unique minimizer on \(X\cap B_r(\bar x)\) and therefore is isolated within that neighborhood's minimizer set.

notation.meaning: Open Euclidean ball of radius r centered at the reference point.

children.title: Local Stability Consequences
children.top_down_role: Perturbation behavior associated with growth plus isolation.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Stability Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic growth yields a quantitative localization bound for minimizers over a fixed neighborhood under uniformly small objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(f,g:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\bar x\in X\). Suppose that, for some \(\alpha>0\) and \(r>0\),
\[
f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\alpha\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^2
\quad\text{for every }x\in X\cap B_r(\bar x).
\]
Let \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and suppose
\[
\lvert g(x)-f(x)\rvert\le\varepsilon
\quad\text{for every }x\in X\cap B_r(\bar x).
\]
If \(x_g\in X\cap B_r(\bar x)\) minimizes \(g\) over \(X\cap B_r(\bar x)\), then
\[
\alpha\lVert x_g-\bar x\rVert^2
\le f(x_g)-f(\bar x)
\le 2\varepsilon,
\]
and consequently
\[
\lVert x_g-\bar x\rVert\le\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\alpha}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every minimizer of the perturbed objective over the specified neighborhood lies within distance square root of two epsilon divided by alpha from the quadratic-growth minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has quadratic growth with modulus \(\alpha>0\) on \(X\cap B_r(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_g-ar x\rVert\le\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\alpha}\).

notation.meaning: Open Euclidean ball of radius r centered at the reference point.

children.title: Degenerate Critical-Direction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Semidefinite but non-strict curvature regimes not resolved by the classical sufficient condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Critical-Direction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero curvature on a nonzero critical direction is the boundary of the classical strict second-order test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a twice differentiable constrained problem at a KKT point \(\bar x\) with Lagrangian \(L\) and critical cone \(C(\bar x)\), assume
\[
d^{\mathsf T}\nabla_{xx}^2L(\bar x)d\ge0
\quad\text{for every }d\in C(\bar x),
\]
but equality holds for some \(d\in C(\bar x)\setminus\{0\}\). Then the strict critical-cone condition fails. The semidefinite test alone establishes neither quadratic growth nor isolation; higher-order feasible geometry or an exact analysis along zero-curvature directions is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative critical-cone curvature with a nonzero zero-curvature direction lies outside the strict sufficient condition and does not by itself ensure isolation.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is a KKT point with a well-defined critical cone \(C(\bar x)\).
The Lagrangian Hessian is positive semidefinite, but not positive definite, on \(C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The classical strict second-order sufficient condition is inconclusive at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Lagrangian of the constrained quadratic program.
Critical cone at the KKT point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary interpretation is plausible, but the applicable constrained second-order theorem depends on constraint qualifications, the critical-cone definition, and multiplier selection. An authoritative source stating the precise version is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flat Critical Rays in Polyhedral Quadratic Programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-constraint consequence of a zero-curvature critical direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Qx+c^\top x\) on \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ Gx\le h\}\), suppose \(d\ne0\) satisfies \(Ad=0\), \(G_i d\le0\) for every inequality active at \(\bar x\), \(\nabla f(\bar x)^\top d=0\), and \(d^\top Qd=0\). Then for some \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\bar x+td\in P\) and \(f(\bar x+td)=f(\bar x)\) for \(0\le t\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-curvature critical ray of a polyhedral QP gives an exactly flat feasible segment.
assumptions_latex: \(d\ne0\) is a critical direction at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nontrivial flat feasible segment starts at \(\bar x\), precluding isolation if \(\bar x\) is locally minimizing.
review_flags: The result is correct, but the established Flatness-Induced Nonisolation node is its canonical theorem home.
knowledge_statements.title: Flat Critical Rays in Polyhedral Quadratic Programs

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is the semidefinite, non-strict boundary where the classical sufficient condition is inconclusive. The proposed affine flat-ray theorem is deferred as duplication of Flatness-Induced Nonisolation. Strict curvature belongs to its sibling, and growth and stability consequences belong to the quadratic-growth family.

children.title: Stationary-Point Landscape
children.top_down_role: The local configurations that motivate global rather than purely stationary analysis.

children.title: Strict-Saddle Escape Geometry
children.top_down_role: Stationary points admitting feasible negative-curvature directions.

children.title: Strict-Saddle Geometry
children.top_down_role: Stationary configurations possessing feasible negative curvature.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative Curvature Does Not Imply Two-Sided Saddle Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology boundary between the negative-eigenvalue convention and a classical two-sided saddle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), the origin is stationary and \(\nabla^2f(0)=-I\) has negative eigenvalues, but \(f(x)<f(0)\) for every \(x\ne0\). Hence the origin is a strict local maximum, not a two-sided geometric saddle. A convention based only on a negative Hessian eigenvalue therefore includes strict maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative curvature alone can describe a strict maximum rather than a two-sided saddle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The origin has negative curvature but is a strict local maximum rather than a two-sided saddle.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative Curvature Does Not Imply Two-Sided Saddle Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Sided Geometry of an Unconstrained Quadratic Saddle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-independent characterization for unconstrained stationary quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), and suppose \(Q\bar x+c=0\). Every neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contains a point below \(f(\bar x)\) iff \(Q\) has a negative eigenvalue. Every neighborhood contains points both below and above \(f(\bar x)\) iff \(Q\) is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative curvature produces arbitrarily close lower points, while indefinite curvature is necessary and sufficient for genuine two-sided saddle geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nearby lower values exist iff \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)<0\), and nearby lower and higher values exist iff \(Q\) is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Geometry of an Unconstrained Quadratic Saddle
Strict-Saddle Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constrained strict-saddle geometry is defined through a realizable critical direction of negative Lagrangian curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A KKT point \(\bar x\) of a twice differentiable constrained problem is a strict saddle if there exist a nonzero critical direction \(d\in C(\bar x)\), a feasible twice differentiable arc \(x(t)\) with \(x(0)=\bar x\) and \(x'(0)=d\), and associated KKT multipliers such that
\[
d^{\mathsf T}\nabla_{xx}^2L(\bar x)d<0.
\]
For an unconstrained quadratic \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), this reduces to \(Q\) having a negative eigenvalue at a stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict saddle has a feasible critical direction with strictly negative second-order Lagrangian curvature; unconstrained quadratics require a negative Hessian eigenvalue.
assumptions_latex: The chosen critical direction is tangent to a feasible twice differentiable arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a locally realizable direction of strictly negative second-order curvature at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Critical cone at the stationary point.
Lagrangian for fixed associated KKT multipliers.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unconstrained specialization is standard, but the proposed constrained strict-saddle definition is multiplier- and feasibility-regularity-dependent and is not a universally standard definition. A precise sourced convention is needed.

children.title: Negative-Curvature Escape
children.top_down_role: Feasible curvature structures permitting departure from strict saddles.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible critical ray with negative quadratic curvature gives an explicit local descent escape.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), and let \(\bar x\in X\). Suppose \(d\ne0\), \(\bar x+td\in X\) for every sufficiently small \(t\in[0,\delta]\), \(\nabla f(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d=0\), and \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0\). Then
\[
f(\bar x+td)-f(\bar x)=\tfrac12t^2d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0
\]
for every sufficiently small \(t>0\). Thus \(\bar x\) is not a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible ray with zero first-order change and negative quadratic curvature immediately decreases the objective and escapes the stationary point.
assumptions_latex: The ray \(\bar x+td\) is locally feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x+td)<f(\bar x)\) for all sufficiently small \(t>0\), so \(\bar x\) is not locally minimizing.

notation.meaning: Symmetric Hessian of the quadratic objective.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.4 Approximation of Critical Points within the Subspace p. 99

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2.4 Approximation of Critical Points within the Subspace p. 99

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of local negative-curvature decrease over a complete feasible ray segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the seed assumptions, suppose \(\bar x+td\) is feasible for every \(t\in[0,t_{\max}]\), \(\nabla f(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}d=0\), and \(d^{\mathsf T}Qd<0\). Then \(t\mapsto f(\bar x+td)\) is strictly decreasing for \(t>0\). If \(t_{\max}<\infty\), the segment minimum occurs at \(t_{\max}\). If the entire ray is feasible, then \(f(\bar x+td)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-slope negative-curvature quadratic decreases along its entire feasible ray; an unbounded feasible ray certifies unboundedness below.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x+td\) is feasible on the stated segment or ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The far endpoint minimizes a bounded feasible ray segment, while an unbounded feasible ray makes the objective unbounded below.

notation.meaning: Largest parameter in the stated feasible ray segment.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Segment and Unbounded-Ray Consequences

children.title: Constraint-Blocked Escape
children.top_down_role: Cases where ambient negative curvature fails to yield a feasible escape direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced-Curvature Criterion for Affine Constraint Blocking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of usable curvature under affine equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b\}\), where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), and suppose \(A\bar x=b\) and \(Q\bar x+c+A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\). If \(\operatorname{range}Z=\ker A\), then \(f(\bar x+Zp)-f(\bar x)=\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Z^{\mathsf T}QZp\). Thus every feasible negative-curvature escape is blocked iff \(Z^{\mathsf T}QZ\succeq0\). In that case \(\bar x\) is a constrained global minimizer; if \(Z^{\mathsf T}QZ\succ0\), it is a strict constrained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under affine equalities only reduced Hessian curvature is usable; ambient negative eigenvectors are harmless when the reduced Hessian is positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: The columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible negative curvature is absent iff \(Z^{\mathsf T}QZ\succeq0\); positive definiteness yields strict constrained minimality.

notation.meaning: Basis matrix for feasible displacement directions.
Reduced Hessian on the affine feasible space.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Curvature Criterion for Affine Constraint Blocking

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Family of Line Constraints Blocking Ambient Negative Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric constrained quadratics where an ambient negative eigendirection is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\) and impose \(y=\alpha x\) with \(|\alpha|<1\). The Hessian has a negative eigenvalue, but every feasible point has \(f(x,\alpha x)=(1-\alpha^2)x^2\). Hence the origin is a strict constrained minimizer despite ambient negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any line of slope strictly between minus one and one blocks the negative eigendirection of the saddle quadratic and makes the origin a strict constrained minimum.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(\{(x,y):y=\alpha x\}\) with \(|\alpha|<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\) is a strict constrained minimizer although \(\nabla^2f\) has a negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.title: A Family of Line Constraints Blocking Ambient Negative Curvature
Constraint-Blocked Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient negative curvature need not provide descent when constraints exclude every corresponding direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min\{f(x,y)=x^2-y^2:(x,y)\in X\},
\qquad X=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y=0\}.
\]
At \(\bar z=(0,0)\), \(\nabla f(\bar z)=0\), and the Hessian \(\operatorname{diag}(2,-2)\) has negative curvature in direction \((0,1)\). That direction is infeasible, while every feasible point is \((x,0)\) and satisfies \(f(x,0)=x^2\ge0=f(\bar z)\). Hence \(\bar z\) is a strict constrained minimizer despite ambient negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative curvature can be unusable: restricting the saddle quadratic to the line y=0 makes the origin a strict constrained minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\) is a strict constrained minimizer although \(\nabla^2f(0,0)\) has a negative eigenvalue.

notation.meaning: Linear feasible set that blocks the negative-curvature direction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and fits the terminal container, but the record supplies no citation or explicit standard-field rationale as evidence.

children.title: Degenerate Stationary-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Neutral-curvature configurations with ambiguous local classification.

children.title: Nonisolated Stationary Sets
children.top_down_role: Continua or clusters of stationary candidates.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Stationary Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For an unconstrained quadratic, singularity produces an affine stationary set whenever the stationarity equation is consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\). If \(Qx_0+c=0\), then the complete stationary set is
\[
\mathcal S=\{x:Qx+c=0\}=x_0+\ker Q.
\]
Consequently, \(\mathcal S\) is nonisolated exactly when \(\ker Q\ne\{0\}\). If the linear system \(Qx=-c\) is inconsistent, the quadratic has no stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent singular quadratic has an affine family of stationary points equal to one solution plus the Hessian kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(Qx_0+c=0\), the stationary set is \(x_0+\ker Q\), and it is nonisolated iff \(Q\) is singular.

notation.meaning: Null space of the quadratic Hessian.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and Dimension of the Stationary Affine Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent solvability tests and dimension formula for the stationary set of an unconstrained quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), the following are equivalent: \(\{x:Qx+c=0\}\ne\varnothing\), \(-c\in\operatorname{range}Q\), and \(c\perp\ker Q\). When they hold, every solution \(x_0\) gives \(\mathcal S=x_0+\ker Q\) and \(\dim\mathcal S=\dim\ker Q=n-\operatorname{rank}Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationary points exist exactly when the linear term is orthogonal to the Hessian kernel; the stationary affine set then has dimension equal to the Hessian nullity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stationarity is solvable iff \(-c\in\operatorname{range}Q\), equivalently \(c\perp\ker Q\), and the stationary-set dimension is \(n-\operatorname{rank}Q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Existence and Dimension of the Stationary Affine Set

children.title: Degenerate Stationary Points
children.top_down_role: Stationary candidates with neutral or insufficient curvature information.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Stationary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained quadratic stationarity is degenerate when the Hessian has a nontrivial null space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), a stationary point \(\bar x\) is degenerate if
\[
Q\bar x+c=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\ker Q\ne\{0\}.
\]
For every \(z\in\ker Q\), one then has \(\nabla f(\bar x+z)=0\) and \(f(\bar x+z)=f(\bar x)\). Thus a degenerate stationary point of an unconstrained quadratic belongs to a nonisolated affine stationary set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic stationary point is degenerate when its Hessian is singular; every null-space displacement is stationary and preserves the objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) and the quadratic is unconstrained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\ker Q\ne\{0\}\), then \(\bar x+\ker Q\) is a nonisolated constant-value stationary set.

notation.meaning: Null space of the Hessian matrix.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Classification of Degenerate Quadratic Stationary Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact inertia classification for a stationary unconstrained quadratic with singular Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), and suppose \(Q\bar x+c=0\) and \(\ker Q\ne\{0\}\). Then \(f(\bar x+d)-f(\bar x)=\tfrac12d^{\mathsf T}Qd\). Hence \(\bar x\) is a nonstrict global minimizer iff \(Q\succeq0\), a nonstrict global maximizer iff \(Q\preceq0\), and a saddle point iff \(Q\) is indefinite. If \(Q=0\), every point is simultaneously a global minimizer and maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate stationary quadratic is classified exactly by Hessian inertia; the zero Hessian gives a constant objective and belongs to both semidefinite cases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inertia of \(Q\) exactly determines the global minimum, global maximum, or saddle classification, with overlap of the minimum and maximum cases when \(Q=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Classification of Degenerate Quadratic Stationary Points

children.title: Stationary-Manifold Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local geometric organization of nonisolated stationary families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent-Normal Geometry of a Quadratic Stationary Manifold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete affine tangent-normal decomposition after the stationarity equation is known to be consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), let \(Qx_0+c=0\), and set \(\mathcal S=x_0+\ker Q\). For every \(x\in\mathcal S\), \(T_x\mathcal S=\ker Q\) and \(N_x\mathcal S=(\ker Q)^\perp=\operatorname{range}Q\). The restriction of \(Q\) to \(N_x\mathcal S\) is nonsingular. If \(z\in T_x\mathcal S\) and \(w\in N_x\mathcal S\), then \(f(x+z+w)-f(x)=\tfrac12w^{\mathsf T}Qw\). Thus the objective is constant tangentially and all nonzero variation is normal to the manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stationary manifold is affine, with Hessian kernel as tangent space and Hessian range as normal space; objective variation occurs only normally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_x\mathcal S=\ker Q\), \(N_x\mathcal S=\operatorname{range}Q\), and \(f\) is constant in tangent directions.

notation.meaning: Tangent space of the affine stationary manifold.
Euclidean normal space of the stationary manifold.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Normal Geometry of a Quadratic Stationary Manifold
Stationary-Manifold Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quadratic stationary manifold is affine, flat along its tangent space, and constant in objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), and suppose \(Qx_0+c=0\). The stationary set
\[
\mathcal S=x_0+\ker Q
\]
is an affine manifold with tangent space
\[
T_x\mathcal S=\ker Q
\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal S.
\]
Moreover,
\[
f(x_0+z)=f(x_0)
\quad\text{for every }z\in\ker Q,
\]
and, for every \(v\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
f(x_0+v)-f(x_0)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}Qv.
\]
Thus the quadratic has zero curvature along the tangent directions \(\ker Q\), while any nonzero curvature occurs in directions outside that kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stationary set of a consistent singular unconstrained quadratic is an affine manifold whose tangent space is the Hessian kernel; the objective is constant along that manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S=x_0+\ker Q\) is an affine stationary manifold with \(T_x\mathcal S=\ker Q\) for every \(x\in\mathcal S\), and \(f\) is constant on \(\mathcal S\).

notation.meaning: Tangent space of the stationary manifold at x.

children.title: Ambiguous Classification Boundary
children.top_down_role: Neutral-curvature regimes where local-minimum, saddle, or flat classifications remain unresolved.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratically constrained examples with identical vanishing tangent curvature but opposite local classifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y-x^2=0\}\), with objectives \(f_+(x,y)=y^2\) and \(f_-(x,y)=-y^2\). At \(\bar z=(0,0)\), the zero multiplier satisfies KKT for both problems. Moreover, \(T_M(\bar z)=\{(d_x,0):d_x\in\mathbb R\}\), and \(d^\top\nabla_{zz}^2L_+(\bar z,0)d=d^\top\nabla_{zz}^2L_-(\bar z,0)d=0\) for every tangent direction \(d\). Yet on \(M\), \(f_+(x,x^2)=x^4\) and \(f_-(x,x^2)=-x^4\). Thus \(\bar z\) is respectively a strict local minimum and a strict local maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical vanishing first- and second-order tangent data can correspond to a strict minimum or a strict maximum when a quadratic constraint curves the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is the regular quadratic equality manifold \(y=x^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero Lagrangian curvature on the tangent space does not determine the local classification.
knowledge_statements.title: Curved-Constraint Minimum–Maximum Ambiguity
Ambiguous Classification Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing first- and second-order variation along a feasible critical direction defeats strict local classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar x\) be stationary for a constrained quadratic program, and let \(d\ne0\) be a critical direction satisfying
\[
d^{\mathsf T}\nabla_{xx}^2L(\bar x)d=0.
\]
First- and second-order data along \(d\) then provide neither a strict descent direction nor positive quadratic growth. If the straight ray is feasible, the quadratic objective is constant to second order—and exactly constant when its linear and quadratic coefficients along the ray vanish. With curved constraints, feasibility corrections may determine either ascent or descent. Classification therefore requires additional feasible-geometry analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-curvature critical direction leaves strict minimum versus saddle classification unresolved unless the feasible path geometry is analyzed more precisely.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is stationary for a constrained quadratic program.
A nonzero critical direction has zero Lagrangian curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: First- and second-order strict tests do not classify \(\bar x\) without further feasible-geometry information.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Zero Lagrangian curvature is a meaningful degeneracy signal, but conclusions about feasible paths and higher-order corrections require realizability and constraint-regularity hypotheses. A source fixing the precise constrained setting is required.

children.title: Multiple Local Minima
children.top_down_role: Competing locally minimizing basins requiring global comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiple local minima are distinct feasible points, each minimizing the objective within its own neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in X\), with \(k\ge2\), are multiple local minima if for each \(i\) there exists \(r_i>0\) such that
\[
f(x_i)\le f(x)
\quad\text{for every }x\in X\cap B_{r_i}(x_i).
\]
They are competing strict local minima when each inequality is strict for \(x\ne x_i\). Local optimality does not rank their basins globally; a global minimizer among them must attain the smallest objective value, subject also to comparison with all other feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple local minima are distinct points that each minimize locally; identifying a global solution requires comparing their values and all remaining feasible points.
assumptions_latex: There are at least two distinct feasible candidate points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(x_i\) is locally minimizing, while global optimality requires comparison over all of \(X\).

notation.meaning: Open neighborhood ball associated with the ith local minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two Strict Local Minima with Unequal Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A box-constrained indefinite quadratic with competing strict local minima, one globally suboptimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<a<1\), consider \(\min\{f(x,y)=xy+ax:(x,y)\in[-1,1]^2\}\). The corners \(p=(1,-1)\) and \(q=(-1,1)\) are strict local minimizers, with \(f(p)=-1+a\) and \(f(q)=-1-a\). Hence \(p\) is a strict nonglobal local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tilted bilinear box quadratic has two strict corner minima of unequal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1,-1)\) and \((-1,1)\) are strict local minimizers, and \(f(-1,1)<f(1,-1)\).

notation.meaning: Linear tilt separating the two local-minimum values.

knowledge_statements.title: Two Strict Local Minima with Unequal Values

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Excludes Competing Strict Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating competing strict basins from convex optimization on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be convex and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Every local minimizer is global, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_X f\) is convex. Therefore two distinct strict local minimizers cannot exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a convex domain, a convex objective cannot have competing strict local minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every local minimizer is global and distinct strict local minimizers are impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Excludes Competing Strict Local Minima

children.title: Classical Trust-Region Subproblem
children.top_down_role: Norm-bounded indefinite quadratic minimization and its spectral optimality structure.

children.title: Secular-Spectral Trust-Region Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Equivalent spectral routes to globally solving the trust-region subproblem.

children.title: Secular Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Scalar spectral characterizations of trust-region global solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Secular Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Euclidean trust-region solutions admit a multiplier characterization and, outside the singular hard case, a scalar secular equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min_{\lVert p\rVert\le\Delta} q(p)
= g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp,
\]
where \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\Delta>0\). A vector \(p_*\) is globally optimal if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\ge0\) such that
\[
(B+\lambda_*I)p_*=-g,
\qquad B+\lambda_*I\succeq0,
\qquad \lVert p_*\rVert\le\Delta,
\qquad \lambda_*(\lVert p_*\rVert-\Delta)=0.
\]
If
\[
\lambda_*>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\},
\]
then \(B+\lambda_*I\) is positive definite and
\[
p_*=-(B+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g.
\]
For a boundary solution in this nonsingular regime, \(\lambda_*\) satisfies the secular equation
\[
\lVert(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\rVert=\Delta.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global Euclidean trust-region step satisfies a positive-semidefinite shifted linear system, primal feasibility, nonnegative multiplier, and complementarity; in the nonsingular boundary case its multiplier solves a scalar secular equation.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(\{p\in\mathbb R^n:\lVert p\rVert\le\Delta\}\) with the Euclidean norm.
The inverse-form secular equation is asserted only when \(B+\lambda_*I\) is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global optimality is equivalent to the displayed multiplier system; when \(B+\lambda_*I\succ0\) and the solution is on the boundary, \(\lambda_*\) satisfies \(\lVert(B+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g\rVert=\Delta\).

source_refs.locator: 5.2.4 Approximation of Critical Points within the Subspace p. 99

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2.4 Approximation of Critical Points within the Subspace p. 99

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity and Uniqueness of the Regular Secular Root
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular active-boundary branch of the Euclidean trust-region problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=U\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)U^{\mathsf T}\), \(\beta=U^{\mathsf T}g\), and \[\psi(\lambda)=\|(B+\lambda I)^{-1}g\|_2^2-\Delta^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\beta_i^2}{(d_i+\lambda)^2}-\Delta^2\] for \(\lambda>\lambda_0:=\max\{0,-d_1\}\). If \(g\ne0\), then \[\psi'(\lambda)=-2\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\beta_i^2}{(d_i+\lambda)^3}<0.\] Hence the regular secular equation has at most one root. If \(\lim_{\lambda\downarrow\lambda_0}\psi(\lambda)>0\), it has exactly one root because \(\psi(\lambda)\to-\Delta^2\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the positive-definite shift domain, the squared-norm secular function is strictly decreasing, so a regular boundary multiplier is unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regular secular equation has at most one root and has exactly one when its lower-end limit is positive.

notation.meaning: Eigenvalues of B in nondecreasing order.
Gradient coefficients in an orthonormal eigenbasis.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity and Uniqueness of the Regular Secular Root

children.title: Eigenvalue Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Matrix-spectral characterizations of trust-region global solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Euclidean-ball trust-region problem with a symmetric, possibly indefinite Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the problem \(\min\{q(x):\|x\|_2\leq\Delta\}\), a feasible point \(x^\star\) is a global minimizer if and only if there exists \(\lambda^\star\geq0\) such that \[(A+\lambda^\star I)x^\star=-a,\qquad A+\lambda^\star I\succeq0,\qquad \lambda^\star(\|x^\star\|_2^2-\Delta^2)=0.\] The spectral condition is equivalently \(\lambda^\star\geq\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(A)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global optimality is equivalent to stationarity, complementary slackness, and a multiplier shift that makes the Hessian positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is globally optimal if and only if the displayed multiplier conditions hold.

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 What Is a Trust-Region Algorithm? p. 1

children.title: Spectral-Route Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between secular plus eigenvalue solution views.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-Route Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence in the regular, nonsingular branch; the hard case is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda>\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(A)\}\). Then \(A+\lambda I\succ0\), and the stationarity equation has the unique solution \(x(\lambda)=-(A+\lambda I)^{-1}a\). A number \(\lambda\) satisfies the boundary secular equation \(\phi(\lambda)=0\) if and only if \((x(\lambda),\lambda)\) satisfies stationarity, positive-semidefinite curvature, complementary slackness, and \(\|x(\lambda)\|_2=\Delta\). Hence either route yields the same regular global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Away from singular shifts, solving the secular equation is equivalent to solving the spectral optimality conditions on the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The secular root and the regular spectral optimality system determine the same primal-dual solution.

children.title: Hard-Case Spectral Boundary
children.top_down_role: Degenerate spectral configurations limiting routine characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Spectral Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular endpoint of the multiplier spectrum for an indefinite classical trust-region problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\lambda^\star=-\theta\), so \(A+\lambda^\star I=A-\theta I\succeq0\) is singular. Singular stationarity is solvable exactly when \(a\perp E\). If \(x_p=-(A-\theta I)^\dagger a\) and \(\|x_p\|_2\leq\Delta\), then every hard-case global minimizer has the form \[x^\star=x_p+z,\qquad z\in E,\qquad \|x_p+z\|_2=\Delta.\] Since \(x_p\perp E\), the final condition is \(\|z\|_2^2=\Delta^2-\|x_p\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the singular multiplier endpoint, an eigenspace component must be added to a pseudoinverse solution to reach the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(\lambda^\star=-\theta\), hard-case minimizers are precisely \(x_p+z\) with the stated eigenspace correction.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Historical Development of Trust-Region Methods p. 8

children.title: Trust-Region Strong Duality
children.top_down_role: Exact dual and semidefinite characterizations for the single-ball regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Strong Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar Lagrangian dual for one Euclidean-ball constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p^\star=\min_{\|x\|_2\leq\Delta}\{x^{\mathsf T}Ax+2a^{\mathsf T}x+c\}\), strong duality holds and \[p^\star=\max_{\substack{\lambda\geq0,\ A+\lambda I\succeq0\\ a\in\operatorname{Range}(A+\lambda I)}}\left\{c-\lambda\Delta^2-a^{\mathsf T}(A+\lambda I)^\dagger a\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(p^\star\) is the largest \(\gamma\) for which some \(\lambda\geq0\) satisfies \[\begin{pmatrix}A+\lambda I&a\\a^{\mathsf T}&c-\lambda\Delta^2-\gamma\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trust-region primal value equals a one-dimensional Lagrangian dual and admits an exact semidefinite characterization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal value equals the Lagrangian dual maximum, with the displayed pseudoinverse representation.

source_refs.locator: 6. Duality in Global Optimization p. 167
1.1 What Is a Trust-Region Algorithm? p. 1

source_witnesses.locator: 6. Duality in Global Optimization p. 167
1.1 What Is a Trust-Region Algorithm? p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Shor SDP for the Classical Trust Region
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted primal semidefinite representation of the single Euclidean-ball trust-region value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[p^\star=\min_{\|x\|_2\le\Delta}\{x^{\mathsf T}Ax+2a^{\mathsf T}x+c\},\] the semidefinite relaxation \[\begin{aligned}\min_{x,X}\quad&\langle A,X\rangle+2a^{\mathsf T}x+c\\\text{s.t.}\quad&\operatorname{tr}(X)\le\Delta^2,\\&\begin{pmatrix}X&x\\x^{\mathsf T}&1\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\end{aligned}\] has optimal value \(p^\star\). Thus relaxing \(X=xx^{\mathsf T}\) creates no value gap for one Euclidean-ball constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Shor lifting of the classical trust-region problem is value-exact after relaxing the rank-one identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted SDP optimum equals \(p^\star\).
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Shor SDP for the Classical Trust Region

children.title: Trust-Region Hard Case
children.top_down_role: The classical spectral degeneracy requiring special global-solution treatment.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Hard Case
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical hard case for an indefinite Euclidean trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The trust-region problem \(\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Ax+2a^{\mathsf T}x+c:\|x\|_2\leq\Delta\}\) is in the classical hard case when its optimal multiplier is \(\lambda^\star=-\theta\), the shifted matrix \(A-\theta I\) is singular, and \(a\perp E\). Equivalently, the gradient term has no component in the eigenspace where the curvature shift first becomes positive semidefinite, so the usual inverse-based secular parametrization cannot determine the required boundary component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hard case is the singular optimal shift where the linear term is orthogonal to the minimum-eigenvalue eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hard case occurs precisely at the singular shift with the linear term orthogonal to the minimum eigenspace.

children.title: Generalized Trust-Region Inequality Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic minimization over one general quadratic inequality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized trust-region inequality model is minimization of \(f\) over the single quadratic sublevel set \(g(x)\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One general quadratic inequality; neither quadratic is assumed convex.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized trust-region inequality problem is \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{f(x):g(x)\leq0\right\},\] where \(f(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax+2a^{\mathsf T}x+c\) and \(g(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Bx+2b^{\mathsf T}x+d\). The model is feasible when \(\{x:g(x)\leq0\}\neq\varnothing\), and it satisfies the strict-feasibility condition when some \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) obeys \(g(\bar x)<0\). The classical ball model is recovered with \(B=I\), \(b=0\), and \(d=-\Delta^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized trust-region problem minimizes one quadratic over the sublevel set of one other, possibly indefinite, quadratic.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Trust-Region Inequality Models

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value formulation for a strictly feasible generalized trust-region inequality problem with finite value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^\star=\inf\{f(x):g(x)\le0\}\), assume \(g(\bar x)<0\), and suppose \(p^\star\in\mathbb R\). Then \[p^\star=\max_{\lambda\ge0}\inf_x\bigl(f(x)+\lambda g(x)\bigr)=\max_{\gamma,\lambda}\{\gamma:\lambda\ge0,\ M(f+\lambda g-\gamma)\succeq0\},\] where \(M(q)\) is the augmented symmetric matrix satisfying \(q(x)=[x^{\mathsf T},1]M(q)[x^{\mathsf T},1]^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict feasibility makes the scalar Lagrangian dual and its two-scalar semidefinite formulation exact.
assumptions_latex: The primal optimal value is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=\max_{\lambda\ge0}d(\lambda)=\max\{\gamma:\lambda\ge0,\ M(f+\lambda g-\gamma)\succeq0\}\).

notation.meaning: Augmented matrix representing a quadratic polynomial.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Scalar-Multiplier Dual and SDP

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient scalar-multiplier conditions at a feasible candidate under strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(g(\bar x)<0\) for some \(\bar x\), and let \(x^\star\) be feasible. Then \(x^\star\) globally minimizes \(f\) over \(g(x)\le0\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \(\nabla(f+\lambda g)(x^\star)=0\), \(\nabla^2(f+\lambda g)\succeq0\), and \(\lambda g(x^\star)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict feasibility, global minimizers are exactly feasible points admitting a complementary scalar multiplier that makes the quadratic Lagrangian convex and stationary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{g(x)\le0}f(x)\iff\exists\lambda\ge0\) satisfying stationarity, complementary slackness, and \(\nabla^2(f+\lambda g)\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Trust-Region Global-Optimality Characterization

children.title: Generalized Trust-Region Constraint Variants
children.top_down_role: Equality-constrained and two-sided single-quadratic-constraint variants.

children.title: Equality Trust-Region Models
children.top_down_role: Trust-region variants with a single quadratic equality constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality Trust-Region Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic minimization over one exact quadratic level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An equality trust-region model is \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(x):g(x)=\tau\}.\] Its feasible region is the quadratic level set \(L_\tau\). For any \(\Delta>0\), if \(g(x)=\|x\|_2^2\) and \(\tau=\Delta^2\), the feasible set is the sphere of radius \(\Delta\), rather than the ball used by the classical inequality trust-region problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality trust-region model restricts the quadratic objective to one exact quadratic level set, such as a sphere.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are real quadratic functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equality trust-region model minimizes \(f\) over the quadratic level set \(g(x)=\tau\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Quadratic Level Sets Need Not Be Compact
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment boundary separating the sphere specialization from arbitrary quadratic equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty quadratic level set \(L_\tau=\{x:g(x)=\tau\}\) need not be bounded, and a quadratic objective need not have a finite minimum on it. For example, with \(g(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2-x_2^2\), \(\tau=0\), and \(f(x_1,x_2)=-x_1^2-x_2^2\), the feasible rays \((t,t)\) satisfy \(f(t,t)=-2t^2\to-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unlike a positive-radius sphere, an arbitrary quadratic equality can define an unbounded level set on which the objective is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: The equality function is an arbitrary real quadratic rather than the positive-definite sphere function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonemptiness of \(L_\tau\) alone does not imply compactness, attainment, or a finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.title: General Quadratic Level Sets Need Not Be Compact

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence for the Sphere Equality Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment property of the canonical Euclidean equality trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\Delta>0\), the sphere \(S_\Delta=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2=\Delta\}\) is nonempty and compact. Consequently every real quadratic \(q\) attains both a global minimum and a global maximum on \(S_\Delta\), even when its Hessian is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic attains both extrema on a nonempty Euclidean sphere, irrespective of indefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\min_{x\in S_\Delta}q(x)\ne\varnothing\) and \(\arg\max_{x\in S_\Delta}q(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Existence for the Sphere Equality Model

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Optimality on a Euclidean Sphere
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient global characterization for the canonical equality trust-region sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_{\|x\|_2^2=\Delta^2}q(x),\qquad q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Ax+2a^{\mathsf T}x+c,\quad \Delta>0.\] A feasible point \(x^\star\) is a global minimizer if and only if there exists \(\lambda^\star\in\mathbb R\) such that \[(A+\lambda^\star I)x^\star=-a,\qquad A+\lambda^\star I\succeq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point globally minimizes a quadratic on a sphere exactly when a free multiplier gives stationarity and a positive-semidefinite shifted Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is globally optimal if and only if the displayed free-multiplier conditions hold.

notation.meaning: Unrestricted multiplier for the sphere equality.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Optimality on a Euclidean Sphere

children.title: Interval Trust-Region Models
children.top_down_role: Trust-region variants with a two-sided quadratic constraint.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are real quadratic functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interval model minimizes \(f\) over the quadratic band \(\ell\leq g(x)\leq u\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided bounds on one shared quadratic function.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Two-Sided Inequality Constraints p. 164

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interval trust-region model is \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(x):\ell\leq g(x)\leq u\}.\] Although written as the two inequalities \(g(x)-u\leq0\) and \(\ell-g(x)\leq0\), both bounds involve the same scalar quadratic image. The feasible region is the quadratic band \(S_{[\ell,u]}\); it becomes a sublevel set if the lower bound is removed and a level set when \(\ell=u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval trust-region model minimizes a quadratic over points whose shared quadratic constraint value lies between two bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Trust-Region Models

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Two-Sided Inequality Constraints p. 164
source_witnesses.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient global certificate using the endpoint multipliers of a quadratic band.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^\star\) satisfy \(\ell\le h(x^\star)\le u\). If there exist \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\) such that \(L(x)=f(x)+\alpha(h(x)-u)+\beta(\ell-h(x))\) has positive-semidefinite Hessian, \(\nabla L(x^\star)=0\), and \(\alpha(h(x^\star)-u)=0=\beta(\ell-h(x^\star))\), then \(x^\star\) globally minimizes \(f\) over \(\{x:\ell\le h(x)\le u\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is globally certified when endpoint multipliers make its quadratic Lagrangian convex and stationary and satisfy complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x^\star)=\min\{f(x):\ell\le h(x)\le u\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Quadratic Global-Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Bands Need Not Be Convex or Connected
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary geometry distinguishing two-sided quadratic bands from convex trust regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=x^2\), \(\ell=1\), and \(u=4\), \[\{x\in\mathbb R:1\le x^2\le4\}=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2].\] Hence an interval trust-region feasible set may be disconnected and nonconvex even when \(h\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-sided bound on a convex quadratic can form a disconnected, nonconvex shell.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{[1,4]}=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]\) is disconnected and nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Bands Need Not Be Convex or Connected

children.title: Equality-to-Interval Transition
children.top_down_role: Structural changes arising when a fixed quadratic level becomes a permitted interval.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are quadratic and \(\tau\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equality model is the zero-width interval model, and its free multiplier is the difference of the two bound multipliers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic and multiplier transition as an interval collapses to a level set.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Two-Sided Inequality Constraints p. 164
source_refs.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality feasible set satisfies \[\{x:g(x)=\tau\}=\{x:\tau\leq g(x)\leq\tau\}.\] For an interval \([\ell,u]\), the Lagrangian contribution of the bounds is \(\alpha(g(x)-u)+\beta(\ell-g(x))\), with \(\alpha,\beta\geq0\). When \(\ell=u=\tau\), this becomes \((\alpha-\beta)(g(x)-\tau)\). Thus the equality multiplier \(\mu\in\mathbb R\) is represented by \(\mu=\alpha-\beta\), showing why its sign is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Collapsing both interval endpoints to one value produces an equality constraint and converts two nonnegative multipliers into one free multiplier.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality-to-Interval Transition

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Two-Sided Inequality Constraints p. 164

children.title: Single-Constraint Exactness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regularity regimes governing exact treatment of equality or interval variants.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One quadratic inequality admits an exact scalar-multiplier certificate; this guarantee does not automatically extend to distinct additional constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the classical scalar-multiplier exactness guarantee.

source_refs.locator: 6. Duality in Global Optimization p. 167

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a single strictly feasible quadratic inequality, \[g(x)\leq0\Longrightarrow f(x)\geq0\] is equivalent to the existence of \(\lambda\geq0\) such that \(f(x)+\lambda g(x)\geq0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). This scalar-multiplier equivalence is the single-constraint exactness boundary: replacing the premise by several distinct quadratic inequalities is not covered by the classical S-lemma and requires additional structure or a stronger certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict feasibility makes the one-constraint quadratic certificate exact; adding distinct quadratic constraints leaves that theorem's guaranteed regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Constraint Exactness Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 6. Duality in Global Optimization p. 167

children.title: Two-Trust-Region Boundary
children.top_down_role: The transition from single-constraint exactness to more difficult multiple-constraint behavior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly feasible degenerate-quadratic instance showing loss of universal scalar-multiplier necessity with two distinct constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_1(x)=-x_1\), \(g_2(x)=-x_2\), and \(f(x)=x_1x_2\). The system \(g_1(x)\le0,\ g_2(x)\le0\) is strictly feasible and implies \(f(x)\ge0\). Nevertheless, no \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0\) make \(f+\lambda_1g_1+\lambda_2g_2\) globally nonnegative, because its Hessian is \(\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\), which remains indefinite independently of the multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two strictly feasible degenerate quadratic inequalities can imply a quadratic inequality without admitting a certificate formed from two nonnegative scalar multipliers.
assumptions_latex: Affine functions are admitted as degenerate quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((g_1\le0\land g_2\le0)\Rightarrow f\ge0\), but \(\nexists\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0\) with \(f+\lambda_1g_1+\lambda_2g_2\ge0\) on \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Constraint Scalar S-Procedure Failure

assumptions_latex: \(f,g_1,g_2\) are real quadratic functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two-multiplier certificate remains sufficient but is not guaranteed necessary by the classical S-lemma.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of the universal classical S-lemma guarantee with two distinct quadratic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If there exist \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\geq0\) such that \[f(x)+\lambda_1g_1(x)+\lambda_2g_2(x)\geq0\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb R^n,\] then \(f(x)\geq0\) whenever \(g_1(x)\leq0\) and \(g_2(x)\leq0\). The converse is not supplied by the classical S-lemma: two distinct quadratic constraints need not admit an exact certificate using only two nonnegative scalar multipliers. Exactness therefore requires separately stated structural or dimensional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With two quadratic constraints, scalar multipliers still certify validity, but the classical one-constraint theorem no longer guarantees necessity.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Trust-Region Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sufficient direction is immediate and the limitation of the classical one-constraint S-lemma is plausible, but no source is supplied for the asserted non-necessity with two distinct quadratic constraints. A precise theorem or counterexample locator is required.

children.top_down_role: Quadratic alternative principles organizing exactness, duality, and their failure boundaries.
